speechtext:
That the Select Standing Committee on Agriculture and Colonization have leave to>
sit during the sittings of this House.

That question was before the Committee on Agriculture, but it was held in abeyance. There was no recommendation from the committee. We did not recommend that such a thing should be done ; therefore, the House is not likely to consent to it.

I am not aware that there is anything in the rules of the House which prevents us from making this motion directly to the House. It is the permission of the House that is required, and I do not understand that it requires an absolute recommendation from the committee. The necessity of it was recognized in the committee. There was more or less apparent obstruction in the committee this morning, the session is drawing to a close, there is a good deail of work to do yet, and from all appearances that work is going to take a good deal of time. It is simply to gain a day that this motion is made. It is perfectly reasonable and it is not in contravention i of any rule or precedent of the House.

But tlie committee have not asked it, and precedent to the House granting that privilege there has always been a request from the committee. The House have never done it without a request from the committee. The committee have not requested it.

A resolution to this effect was moved in the committee this morning but before it could be put to the committee some one called out ' eleven o'clock,' and insisted that the committee rise, notwithstanding the earnest protest on the part of several members of the committee that the committee could sit until we heard the call-bell of the House. The committee rose and the chairman did not put the resolution. It is impossible to get through with the business of the Agriculture Committee in a short session from 9.30 to 11 o'clock, because any matter can be debated to such an extent that it will be impossible to arrive at any conclusion as happened this morning* and as happened at the last meeting of the committee.

Mr. Speaker, I think that the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) wall conclude that it is the privilege of the committee to debate any question as they think proper. But, to coma here when there is no recommendation from the committee which should be the judge whether we should extend the hours of sitting or not is quite unprecedented. The right hon. leader of the government knows well that it is always an awkward thing to have eleven o'clock sittings when there remains some unfinished work to be done by the committees. There is an hour and a half, if the chairman desires to call the committee earlier, in which the committee may sit. Until there is a recommendation from the committee itself that we should absent ourselves from the sitting cf this House it seems to me an extraordinary proceeding that any hon. gentleman should propose to have the committee sit during the period that members are obliged to be in their places here. I will not reflect in the least upon the objects that hon. gentlemen have in view in this proceeding, but if 1 were to do so it would not be very complimentary. I hope the right hon. Prime Minister will not, for the purpose of serving any end on one side or the other, permit such an outrage as to compel, without the recommendation of the committee, members to absent themselves for one duty or another by the adoption of the proposed motion now before the House. I think it would be a perfect outrage to make a) departure of that kind.

When the hon. gentleman moved his motion in the committee it was three minutes past eleven, and the committee had no opportunity of discussing whether it would be a proper thing or whether it is really necessary to extend the time
of the Agriculture Committee. Personally I do not think it is really necessary to prolong the time of the committee. I think the committee have arrived at that stage in their work that they will be able to arrange their business within the time allotted. T have never before known that two members could come into this House and ask that a committee's time be prolonged in the absence of the decision of the committee upon the point.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say as seconder of this motion that, as was stated by my hon. friend from Annapolis (Mr. Wade), the committee had no opportunity of passing upon this question at all. The resolution was moved in the committee asking the House to grant power to the committee to sit while the House was in session. The resolution was presented at least a quarter of an hour before the House bell rang.
No, three minutes past.

When I came from the committee, down here the Speaker had not yet arrived in the chamber, and it took me some time to come from the committee room to the chamber. We were not allowed to press that motion. My hon. friend from East Eigin (Mr. Ingram) thinks that the work of the committee can be got through without this resolution being passed. If that is the case the resolution will do no harm. If we can get the work through _ bef ore eleven o'clock we will not have to sit after eleven, but if we cannot it is absolutely necessary that we should have this extended time in order that we may get through with the work. The chairman of the committee complained that a large amount of work had accumulated, he said that a report had to be made to the House, that it was getting late in the session- and he appealed to the members to get through with the work. At the last sitting of the committee and at the sitting this forenoon we could get nothing done, and I submit if we do not get this resolution through and have the right to sit during the time the House is in session we will never be able to complete the work, and the House may adjourn without the committee having been able to bring in a report to the House. I do not see that this is an injury to any person. There are enough members who are not interested in the estimates and similar matters to conduct the meetings of the committee. This is not a new suggestion ; I have been in this House for eight years, and nearly every year a resolution of this kind has been passed by the House and committees have sat while the House was in session. The business of the country went on just the same, and in order to facilitate matters and to give an opportunity to complete the labours ol tha, committee I think this resolution should pass.

As chairman o'' the committee, I wish to state to the House as I did to the committee this morning, that a very great deal of business remains to be done by the committee, and the question which at present engages the attention of the committee is one of great importance. The committee has not yet reached that condition of unanimity that would indicate that we shall reach an early conclusion. Personally, as chairman, I am exceedingly anxious that the business of the committee should be got into such shape that we could report to the House at as early a date as possible. This morning I received a motion in the committee, but it was five minutes past eleven, and I had no information from the House that they would not meet until a quarter past eleven, and never decided that X should not press the motion, and so we adjourned at live minutes past eleven. The consequence was that, owing to the obstruction that took place, I was prevented from securing the sanction of the committee in asking for leave to sit while the House was in session.

With reference to the item in connection with the Hillsboro' bridge, I wish to call the attention of the committee to a. letter which appears in the Auditor General's Report. I shall read this letter because not only is it important as regards the particular item, but as regards the position which the government has taken with reference to a great many contracts :
Audit Office, Ottawa, February 12, 1904.
Dear Sir,-My attention has been called recently to the many Orders in Council relieving public works contractors from the' obligation of completing their contracts within the time limit.
From the wording of the orders it. seems that those representing the government in the transactions consider that, while the contractors are accommodated, the government is saved from any loss, because there is not developed by the postponement of the date of completion a means of exacting a heightened charge from the government by the contractor. This seems a manifestly inaccurate conclusion.
When it was determined by the government to have a particular work done, it was concluded that the direct advantage, or the indirect one, or both together, would be at least as great as all the outlay and would, therefore, besides recouping the country for the salaries of the engineers and other servants engaged, reimburse eventually the money paid to contractors, and in the meantime the interest as it would periodically mature.
In the case of a wharf, a bridge, or a railway line, you may have entered into no obligation to provide at a particular time the accommodation to the neighbourhood which the work when completed will afford, but as trustees for the people you came to the conclusion that the completed work would provide to the public an advantage equal in value to the interest on the expenditure-
By the privilege given to the contractor, the country has been deprived of the use of the work for the length of the postponement, while the interest is accumulating each day.
The magnitude of the donations from public funds to contractors will be understood to some extent by considering one of the large works-for instance the Hillsboro' bridge. It was to have been completed on April 8, 1902. The time was first extended to November 30, 1902, later to December 31, 1903, and now to

The effect of this amendment will be to make section 3 of the Railway Act as we now have it read as follows :
This Act shall apply to all persons, and express companies and railways (other than government railways) within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada, and shall be incorporated and construed, as one Act, with the Special Act, subject as herein provided.
Now if my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) will look at section 2 subsection (w) of the Railway Act, the interpretation clause, he will find that:
The expression ' Special Act ' means any Act under which the company has authority to construct or operate a railway, or which is enacted with special reference to such railway, and include all such Acts.
So that this provision would be absolutely unworkable in the Act as we have it. My hon. friend is quite right when he says that this subject has been already considered. It was considered by the special committee that was appointed to look into the Railway Act when it was introduced into this House last session. At that time Boards of Trade, among others the Board of Trade of the city of Toronto, appeared before the committee and urged upon it the desirability of amending the Act so as to make it applicable to express companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

When the Railway Bill was introduced last session Mr. Blair, then Minister of Railways and Canals, and myself were appointed a sub-committee to hear reports made by different public bodies in the country. At that time Boards of Trade, and among these Boards of Trade were members of the Toronto Board of Trade, appeared before the committee and urged upon us that we should include express companies in the Act as my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) suggests at the present time. The point was then argued out fully, as appears by the report of the proceedings, and the conclusion arrived at then was that in the first instance it was doubtful as to whether or not we had the power to regulate the charges of the express companies and that in any event if we had the power many of the provisions of this Act would require to be so amended as to make them applicable to express companies and that such an amendment would be necessary as would practically require the changing of a great number of the sections of the Act.

The amendment in its present form would make the Act absolutely unworkable. When my hou. friend introduced his amendment iu this House the Bill containing that amendment was by agreement referred to the Railway Committee of the House. The matter was there discussed and the conclusion arrived &t by the Railway Committee was that this amendment could not be applied to the Railway Act as we now have it. It may be, and I can conceive that under certain conditions it would be, desirable that express companies should be regulated in some respects by the Railway Commission but it is a question-I will not say a settled question so far as I am concerned-whether we have the power to regulate the contracts made by the express companies. It is quite true that we have the power to incorporate these companies but as to regulating the contracts which they make in different parts of the country that is a question which has not been settled, so far as my knowledge goes, either by judicial determination or by any opinion expressed in any quarter, which I have been able to see.

I have looked into the ease of Parson and the Citizens' Insurance Company, and I would like to give to the committee the result of my reference to that case. The Citizens' Insurance Company was incorporated by the parliament of Canada exactly as the Dominion Express Company was incorporated here. I am not sure whether or not all the express companies were incorporated by us, but I am quite sure that the Dominion Express Company was. The Citizens' Insurance Company was incorporated by the Canadian parliament and the Ontario legislature passed a statute regulating the conditions of insurance contracts, that is the contracts made by insurance companies in Canada. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It does appear to me that it is not the freight of a railway company that we are regulating ; it is the freight carried by the express company and whether that freight is carried by an express company on a railway train or by horse car or by steamer or vessel, the effect would be the same, and I cannot see bow we are to discriminate between that express business which was done on railway trains and the express business done by the ordinary cartage system in the country, or on vessels. Have we any power to regulate the rates charged by the express companies, for instance, on tlie express business done in cities ?

Is not the question whether we have power to regulate the charges for freight upon a railway ? It seems to me that the Dominion, having jurisdiction over a railway company and over its railway, can regulate all charges for everything that is carried upon that railway, and I do not see any difficulty in that respect whether the railway company is handling the stuff itself or has put up an intermediary between itself and the public.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Is it the contract between the express company and the railway company that we are asked to regulate or the contract between the express company and the private individual ? That is the distinction. It is with respect to that particular contract between the express company and the individual that I expressed my doubt as to the power to regulate. Would my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) permit me to draw attention to this fact, which I shall illustrate by an example ? Take express freight coming say from Port Arthur to Collingwood, by vessel, then from Collingwood to Toronto by rail and from the railway station in Toronto to the warehouse of the merchants by carts. What part of the express charge which is made upon the freight from Port Arthur to the

merchants' warehouse in Toronto would we be able to regulate ? Can we regulate the express charge from Port Arthur to Oollingwood hy vessels ? Undoubtedly not. Can we regulate the charge for its conveyance in vehicles in the streets of Toronto ? Undoubtedly not. How can we regulate the matter ?
Where does the power to regulate these charges lie ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In the provincial legislature.
Do we not find every day ordinary freight shipped from Port Arthur to Collingwood by water, thence by rail to Toronto and then delivered by cart in Toronto ? And yet we cap regulate freight charges ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: When the freight is carried by a railway company, that is under our jurisdiction. We say to that company: The charge you make on that freight is determined by us ; you adopt any method you choose to deliver it. But why should a contract made between an express company and an individual be under different jurisdiction from a contract made by any other corporation under provincial jurisdiction ?

I will tell you the reason. When we give existence to a company, we can give it on any conditions we like. When we give a company the right to carry parcels by express or otherwise, we can say that it shall only charge for carrying those parcels what the commission says is a right charge. Surely that is within our power. If we have a right to give a company its corporate existence, we can give it that existence on any conditions we like. As to freight canned partly by water and partly by rail, we have taken power under the Railway Act to regulate that. The commission can consider what are the proper proportions of the charge to be apportioned to the water, to the railway, and to carrying by horses in a city. That is one of the conditions of our Railway Act. Whether we have the power or not, it was urged upon us by Mr. Blair, who introduced the Act, that that was an essential in the regulation of rates ; otherwise a railway company could apportion so large a proportion of the charge to the water' carriage as to do away with all regulations in reference to carrying by rail.

I must say I have not given this question very much study or examination as yet. but I am inclined to support the Minister of Justice. This is a question as to the power of this parliament to regulate the rates of express companies. It seems to me. speaking off-hand, without having given the subject very much consideration. that it is a matter of regulating a contract within the province ; and I really
cannot understand, unless there is some power given to us by the British North America Act, how we can regulate the rates of carriage by express companies any more than we can regulate the rate of carriage by individuals within the different provinces. It is not because this parliament has given existence to a company that it has a right to interfere in the contracts made by that company. My hon. friend who has just taken his seat says that we can impose as a condition of giving the charter the regulation of the rates which are to be charged by the corporation. I must distinguish here. I will not say that if. upon the application of certain parties for incorporation, the charter contained the condition that the rates are to be regulated by the charter itself, this would not be within the authority of the granting power ; but to make a general law applicable to all corporations which are to come into existence hereafter hy charters of the Dominion parliament. and to say that this should apply to contracts made by them, is a broad statement which I am not at present ready to accept, and I cannot go as far as my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Haggart). There is another argument put forward here, which is an argument ab inconvienti. My hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) says, if I understand him rightly, that we should have the power of regulating the rates charged by express companies, because we have the power of regulating rates upon railways. I do not think that is a conclusion to be necessarily arrived at. It may be inconvenient. It may be that the law or the constitution is not complete on that point. But the line is drawn. We are given by the constitution the power of regulating rates on railways. If a coTnpany not being a railway company is called into existence, and does a part of the work that generally falls to railway companies, that is not a reason for extending the powers given by the constitution to this House. It may be for the very reason that the power of regulating rates on railways is given to the parliament of Canada by the constitution, that express companies are created so that the rates may not be regulated ; but I do not see the force of the argument of my hon. friend. Now, this is a question of some importance, and it seems to me that a great deal of precaution should be exercised before we enact such a law. For my part, I have not heard of any great agitation in the country calling for such legislation. It may exist in some parts of the country, particularly in that part from which my hon. friend comes; but I do not think the general public has been suffering to such an extent from the rates charged by express companies that we should legislate in a hurry upon this important question.

I might point out for the information of the hon. gentleman who has junt spoken that the fruit-growers of Ontario feel very severely the charges of the express companies. The shipment of fresh fruit from Ontario to the west is a great and growing business, the people of the west wish to get the fresh fruit of Ontario, and the regulation of these express charges means getting or not getting the market. If what the hon. Minister of Justice and the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) say is true, it means that the railways can evade the whole Railway Act by turning all their freight business over to the express companies. Suppose the argument of the Minister of Justice is true, a declaration of this parliament that the railway companies shall do their own express business would bring them under the Railway Act. That can be done in two lines. They can be prohibited from turning over their express business to other companies. It is all an evasion-an attempt to get away from what hon. gentlemen opposite promised the country. They promised a tribunal which would regulate all charges on freights in this country, which would protect the farmer and the fruit-grower,' and would see that no unfair discrimination was practised in the matter of charges by these common carriers. If my proposal is unconstitutional, it can be made constitutional in one minute. But I do not believe it is unconstitutional. I agree with the opinion of the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Haggartl given here to-day. I believe these companies are quite within the jurisdiction of this parliament to-day.

My hon. friend might substantiate that statement. I do uot wish to take up a great deal of time on this amendment, as there are others to come on. But I wish to point out to the Minister of Justice that I think his constitutional contention is merely a legal quibble. I believe ways can be found to bring tbe express companies within the jurisdiction of the'Railway Commission. I have suggested one way, namely, that every company be compelled to do an express business, and be not allowed to contract itself out of its obligations in that matter. That avoids the entire question of law, and ail the question of constitutional interpretation raised by the Minister of Justice. But there is another way-and I am glad to see the Postmaster General is in his place at this time. The other way to regulate express charges in this country is by the government taking over the express business and extending the postal and parcel post system. We on this continent are away behind the continent of Europe in the development of the express business. Let me tell you what they do in Germany. I am reading now an extract from the ' Cosmopolitan Magazine : '
While we (the United States) absolutely refuse to accept a package greater than four pounds in weight, Germany has found it good business to extend the limit to 110 pounds. These 110 pounds will he sent by the German

government from one end of Germany to the other for 30 cents, or about one-fourth of a cent per pound.
But even that is not all. When it arrives at its destination, the 110 pound package is delivered at the home.
And that is not all. For from two to six cents extra, the government insures the package and guarantees its safe delivery.
And again, even this much is not all. If, Instead of to Germany, a merchant in a city of North Germany wishes to ship a package of one hundred and ten pounds to a city in the southernmost prJH of Austria, he may do even this for thirty cents, about one-fourth of a cent a pound-that is, the merchants of Rochester pay six thousand per cent more to the United States government for sending parcels from Rochester to Buffalo, than do the Germans even to the extreme limits of a foreign country.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext: Who writes that ?

John Brisben Walker, editor of the ' Cosmopolitan Magazine,' who has made a great study of this question. The reason, as Mr. Walker points out, why this parcel post system has not been expanded in the United .States is because of the domination and supremacy of the express companies, and I will give my authority for that, namely, Mr. John Wana-maker. recently Postmaster General of the United States. When Mr. Wanamaker was asked why the express system in the United States had not been improved, how it was that the postal department had not been brought up to date with England, with Germany and all these other countries, his reply was as follows :
There are four reasons why we have not a parcel post system like they have in Germany. The first of these is the Adams Express Company ; the second is the American Express Company ; the third, the Wells-Fargo Express Company ; and the fourth, the Southern Express Company.
Now what I charge here is that not only do the express companies seek, and so far successfully, to avoid a control of their rates by some public body, but they are equally powerful in this country as they are in the United States, and to-day they prevent and hinder the expansion of our parcel post system into a system such as they have in England and in Germany. And yet they have been out and out opponents of the parcel post system in the United States, as I believe they are here to-day. At any rate, they are to-day on evidence in our Railway Committee as objecting to a public regulation of their charges. I guarantee that I will bring suit myself ; if the hon. gentleman will give me a chance to show where the power lies, I will undertake an
action, I can get the Board of Trade of Toronto to undertake an action. This is not the first time this question has been raised in the House. The hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Kemp), myself, and some others, last session wlieu the Bill first wrent through, fought this matter out, and suggested then that the express companies come within the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission. Now I leave the case to the House and to t-he country. You can do what you like with me in this matter. I may be successful in committee, and I may not he. In considering this question, the committee must bear in mind that a much larger proportion of goods that Canadian people now consume are sent by express than was the case some year ago. It will be remembered that in Canada at this moment there is a centralization of business. Manufacturers are centralizing their business, merchants are uniting their small businesses into larger ones, and thus trading places are getting further away from the consumer than they were years ago.
Thus I think it is only fair that some effort should be made by the parliament o'

6704 '
Canada to enable the consumers to get cheaper express rates than they have at tills moment. You will bear in mind that the farmers of Canada, particularly the farmers of the older provinces, are engaged almost entirely in a different occupation from that in which they were engaged some years ago. There are many farmers in the province of Ontario and in the province of Quebec-I speak particularly for the province of Ontario-who send their total output of *butter, eggs and poultry to market by express. You will remember also that the creamery industry is largely carried on, and that almost every gallon of cream that is sent to the leading centres is sent by express. I repeat what I said before, that the farmers of the country should get cheaper express rates than they do at the present time. Then the manufacturers are particularly interested in the cheapening of express rates, for the reason that in the summer time, when the farmers are busily engaged with their farming operation, they send a great many of their products, such as binder twine and other manufactured articles to meet the necessities of the farmers, by express. Therefore, the consumers ail over'Canada are interested in the reduction of express rates. The government have thought it to be their duty to appoint a Railway Commission at a very large expense to the people. This expense the people are not condemning, but they are awaiting the results of the work of this commission. and wlien the commission are investigating the rates charged for sending freight at a slow rate of speed through this country by the different lines of railway, I cannot understand why the government should not be williug, if it is possible, and I think it is possible, to make such changes in the law as will enable the Railway Commission to regulate express rates and give the consumers Icheaper rates than those which they have to pay at the present time. I do not wish to go into a detailed statement of the question. That is unnecessary, as my hon. friend from East York (Mr. "Maclean) has pointed out the facts at some length, not only this session, but last year a-s well. The government have had at least one year's notice. I do not complain against the hon. Minister of Justice in saying that another year should pass before this question is dealt with, but if another year passes by and we are no closer to the result than we are this year, after having given notice a year ago, I do not think the case is very strong to show that we should wait for another year. I am of the opinion that at [DOT]this session we should make such a change in the law, either by the adoption or the amendment of my hon. friend from East York, or by the adoption of such a modified amendment as will place the regulation of all express charges on the different lines of railways altogether under the control of the Railway Commission.

Mr. Speaker, as X am unable to support the amendment moved by my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean), and as I do not care to give a silent vote on it, because it seems to me that there are several amply sufficient reasons why at the present time the amendment should not be carried, I venture to trespass upon the attention of the House for a few moments. I admit that when my hon. friend was speaking on his amendment he gave us some very interesting information and pointed out some things that my hon. friend the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) and my hon. friend the Postmaster General tSir William Mulock) might do, but after all the suggestions were something like the Gowers that bloom in the spring-they had nothing to do with the case. I understand that the question before the House is whether or not a certain clause in the Railway Act is to be amended by giving power to the Railway Commission to deal with express companies. Whether or not the hon. Postmaster General should take over this branch of the service is another question altogether, and can be considered at another time. Rut, in the meantime, if, as business men, we apply ourselves to the question before the House, it seems to me there are ample reasons to justify us in declining to support the amendment. Only a year has elapsed since the Railway Act was threshed out to a great extent in this House. In the province of Ontario we have been complaining that there is too much legislation, that a statute is put on the statute-book, and that before the people or the lawyers have had time to understand what has been enacted changes are introduced. X venture to believe that a strong case of necessity should be made out before, the very first year after we have passed an Act to amend the Railway Act and while its provisions are being tried, we should endeavour to change it again. But there is another point. I think it is only fair to remember that in the passing of Bills through this House the Minister of Justice occupies a peculiar position. In one sense he is responsible for all the legislation that passes. If a measure, no matter from what side of the House it may come, is passed by this House and not opposed by the Minister of Justice, who is the head of the legal department in the Honse. and if afterwards that legislation is held to be ultra vires, it is, to a certain extent, a reflection on the Minister of Justice. It does seem to me that, when an amendment such as this is introduced, when the hon. Minister of Justice says that in his judgment it is very doubtful if we have the p-ower to pass such an amendment, and when. I venture to say, there is not one lawyer in the House who would stake his 1 reputation and say with certainty that there are no grounds for the position which the bon. Minister of Justice takes, a very great responsibility would be thrown upon us if
It would be -a good thing for the lawyers.

If I were as selfish as some people that might appeal to me, but I am speaking as a representative of the people, not as a lawyer or the representative of lawyers, and I think my hon. friend will give me credit at all events for sincerity in occupying that position. It has been said that if this matter is allowed to stand for a year the law will not be changed, it will be the same as it is now at the end of the year, and we will not be any better off. But in the course of a year this matter may be considered. In the course of a year decisions may be given by the courts which will place beyond controversy the question whether we have or have not the power to pass such an amendment as this. In any event, every member of this House will admit, from what we have already seen in the transaction of business by the Railway Commission, that there is ample business, urgent, pressing business, to keep the commission busy
during this year, and it will not be necessary that they should remain idle merely because we decline to throw on them this additional amount of business. The passage of such an amendment as that now proposed would compel the commission to leave undone business which is as important and pressing as that which would thus be put upon them.

Am I correct in the understanding that my hon. friend says that because it is not settled that we have the power, we therefore should not assume that we have the power ? I would ask if that was the usual course followed by Sir Oliver Mowat in his provincial legislation ? Did he not claim, on the other hand, that the proper thing to do was, where there was a semblance of right, to assume that we had the power, then to legislate on these lines and allow the courts to decide if we had or had not the power.

My hon. friend is confusing two things. It is one thing to assume a power, and another thing, -when a piece of legislation is before the House, if the legislature is inclined to think we have not the power, to hold our hands, as we well might do. If the House thought that there was little doubt that we had the power, it would be different.

Does my hon. friend remember that when the McCarthy Act was passed in this House with regard to taking the licenses from the control of the provinces, very eminent legal authorities, including I think Hon. Edward Blake, held that we had not the power. But Sir John Macdonald, after obtaining the opinions of very eminent lawyers, including Mr. Betb-une of Toronto, said that wre had the power, and the House proceeded accordingly.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext: It cost a quarter of a million dollars to find that out.
It was an unfortunate thing for this country that this was done.
It is the principle, not the Act that I am speaking of.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I am not without sympathy for the hon. gentleman who has moved this amendment. Certainly the proposition is worthy of very serious consideration, and, from a selfish standpoint, any one occupying the position of head of the Department of Railways and Canals would rejoice at the passage of such an amendment as is proposed. It would, however, be a very serious matter indeed if we were to enact this as the law of the laud and be met with the difficulties suggested by the Minister of Justice. I think that on general principles it is unwise to tinker with the Railway Act. except in so far as it is absolutely necessary until such time as that Act, especially in connection with the Railway Commission, has been fairly tried.

Reference has been made by the hop. member for Halifax to the question of express privileges on the Intercolonial Railway. He states that he has receivd resolutions from the Halifax Board of Trade. 1 may say that I have received resolutions, not only from that Board of Trade but from many other Boards of Trade in the maritime provinces and petitions by the score have been submitted to me with a view to having the Intercolonial Railway opened to the Dominion Express Company in regard to all trains. At present the Dominion Express Company 'have express privileges on certain trains of the Intercolonial Railway. The proposition now made is that we should give them privileges co-extensive with the privileges enjoyed by the Canadian Express Company. This is a matter of serious moment to the Intercolonial Railway. I sympathize with the desire of many towns and villages along the line of the Intercolonial Railway, whose merchants would wish to have a certain amount of competition, .but it seems to me that such competition would not bring to them the advantages "which they now anticipate. Those places which have that competition have not enjoyed as fully as they anticipated the advantages of the competition which they have secured and I apprehend that those who are now looking towards the accomplishment of the prayer of the petition would perhaps be quite as much disappointed as the others have been, it involves to the Intercolonial Railway serious consequences both as regards its earnings and also as regards the cost of furnishing privileges for all express companies. I think that the Intercolonial Railway is to-day realizing something above $100,000 annually as their share of the profits of the express privileges from the Canadian Express Company. That is on the basis of the Intercolonial Railway securing over its whole line from Moncton to Montreal a percentage of the express rates. Now if a change is made and the Dominion Express Company, a part and parcel,, as my hon. friend says, of the Canadian Pacific Railway, are granted the privileges of the Intercolonial Railway they can go in and secure their trade without any very great advantage to the people, without any lessening of rates, as I understand it, and they can take that express to St. John and thence over their line to western points. In going the other way, they would take it all to St. John, the Intercolonial Railway would get their quota east of St. . John.	Under the present
arrangement the Intercolonial Railway gets its proportion of the whole rate to Montreal because the Intercolonial Railways goes to Montreal. This amendment would therefore affect very materially the earnings of the Intercolonial Railway in connection with express freight. On the other hand the Intercolonial Railway would necessarily have to provide additional car Mr. EMMERSON.
privileges at greater expense. The probabilities are that they would have to run an additional express car on each express train, and therefore, from the standpoint of dollars and cents, the matter has to be viewed by the Railway Department. I have listened to a number of delegations during the present session who have appeared before me with a view to emphasize the desire of the fruit-growers and fish dealers to have these additional express privileges along the line of the Intercolonial Railway. The matter is under consideration. I appreciate the arguments that have been put forward in favour of the idea but I must not be unmindful of the conditions prevailing on the Intercolonial. I would like to see all the railways in Canada, including the Intercolonial Railway, open to all the express companies, and if this were made general, if the Canadian, the American, the Dominion and all the express companies had equal privileges on all the lines throughout the Dominion, there would be many advantages. But if one company reserves to itself the right to monopolize all the express privileges in one section, they should not have the right to enter other sections and share with others that Which they themselves are not willing to grant in their district.
Might I ask my bon. friend how long the contract now existing between the government and the Canadian Express Company has to run ?	,

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It expired in December.	.

Well, I hope the Minister of Railways wTill never surrender to the express companies. I trust that when that contract expires in December, he will establish the Canadian express company belonging to the people of Canada, a national express which he will control. Is it not absurd and the height of impudence for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to come to the Canadian government and say, we want you to let us on your line in competition with other companies, and we refuse to let them on our line ? The Dominion Express Company will not allow any other express comjtany to share the cars with them.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Will my hon. friend pardon me ? I neglected to say that on the Prince Edward Island Railway, which is part of the government system of railways, the railway carries on its own express business.

And so I would like to see it over the whole of the Intercolonial. As I said before, the Grand Trunk is on record as having refused to allow a com-netitive express company to have the use of its cars, and it defeated the other company some years ago, although the other company

acted on the advice of the late Dalton McCarthy. The Grand Trunk is so strong that it prevented that competition, and the Canadian Pacific Kailway is so strong that it can prevent any other company getting on is lines. It was not the business men of the maritime provinces who asked for this express business from the Intercolonial so much as it was the secret agents of the Dominion Express Company, who went through all these towns and drafted the resolutions which were put into the hands of the boards of trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: There is no doubt about that.

These companies are trying to get their fangs on the people's railway. These legal arguments may be made by the Minister of Justice and the hon. member for Essex. They say there will be litigation. Let there be litigation. There is not a public wrong for which there is not a legal remedy ; that is a good maxim in law, I believe. If there is some legal objection in the way, let it be removed. What is needed is not men to get up here and erect men of straw-, and say there is this in the way and that in the way. All these objections can be cleared out of the wjay if it is the intention of parliament to regulate these companies ; and when you find them contracting themselves out of their obligations and out of the jurisdiction of this House, it is high time that we compelled the express companies to come within the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission. In Ontario this express business is something enormous, and it means everything to the farmers and fruit-growers. In the city of Toronto nearly all the milk and fruit that comes in every day in carloads comes by express. The price of milk to the farmers is altogether regulated by the express charges. I know of twenty teams in my own constituency which are every day bringing milk to the city of Toronto for distances of twenty or thirty miles under a broiling sun, with great loss to the milk, because the express companies force it on the roads. In the district of Niagara there was built some years ago a powerful electric line which handled a great deal of fruit; and by reason of a connection between it and the Canadian Pacific Railway, the fruit of the Niagara district was put into the city of Ottawa and the city of Montreal, and even further east. It got to be a great business, and the Canadian Pacific Railway was good enough to accommodate it and give it reduced rates. But the moment the Grand Trunk saw this, its agents went out. They captured the Hamilton and Beamsville trolley line which they hold to-day. and the fruit-growers are at the mercy of the Grand Trunk. It has cut out the Canadian Pacific Railway, and when the proper time comes it will jump up the
express rates and have control of this trade. If there is any legal obstruction in the way of this parliament controlling these express companies, it can easily be removed. Parliament can by its vote to-day put these companies under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission, and by next year, by testing the matter in the courts, we shall know whether they are under the jurisdiction of this parliament or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I would say to my hon. friend that in view of the fact that the relation of the express companies to the Intercolonial will have to be determined by the Governor in Council before next session, they might very well at the same time consider the larger question relating to the express companies throughout Canada. There are in my judgment very strong arguments to be advanced in favour of the contention of my hon. friend. I am quite prepared to admit that ; but I do not think it is opportune at this moment to incorporate his amendment into the Railway Act. We might fairly have it stand over until next year, and the whole question could very properly be determined in connection with the proposition relating to the Intercolonial Railway.
Will the hon. minister ex-* plain to the committee what success has followed the management of the express business of the government road in Prince Edward Island ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I have not had an opportunity of personally going into the question ; but from what I gather from the general manager, there are difficulties in connection with that, because the jurisdiction of the railway ends at Charlottetown or Summerside, as the case may be, and when the express companies on the mainland send articles over to the island an additional express rate has to be paid on the island. It is like a double freight rate, and it is a pretty large sum for the recipient or the shipper of the article. It is simply adding the charge of one company to the charge of another. From that standpoint it is very objectionable to the people of Prince Edward Island, and it is not completely satisfactory to the managers of the railway.
I would like to ask the hon. minister whether there is a system of express under the government administration of the railway in Prince Edward Island ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I have stated that there is a system of express freight on the Prince Edward Island Railway, controlled by the railway management.

The hon. minister says the matter is controlled by the railway management. With respect to parcels going in

there, has not the Dominion Company as good a right as the Canadian Express ? Do yon pretend to say that you take complete control of this express company on the Prince Edward Island Railway ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: There are no express companies which have privileges on the Prince Edward Island Railway.
I understand then that there are no express companies having special privileges on that railway, and that the railway takes full charge of all express business on the island.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: That is correct as I understand it.

Here is another instance where the public get the lean end. The public get the express business in Prince Edward Island, but where that business is profitable it is controlled by private companies. The government has never yet had anything like a fair show. Let the minister take over the whole express business. Let him compel the express companies to give his company as good treatment as they give to each other and there will be a great improvement in the express system in the maritime provinces. We will then have the fish ' of the maritime provinces sent to the west and the fruit of the west taken down to the sea, and there will be a larger building up of trade between the provinces.

In my opinion the express companies should be under the control the Railway Commission, which is the only body we have in Canada capable of dealing with their rates and regulations. But while I am in favour of the principle of the motion of my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean), I think we should hesitate, in view of the doubts expressed by the hon. Minister of Justice, undertaking the serious obligation which my hon. friend wants us to assume. As the Minister of Justice has pointed out, the adoption of this motion would lead to a revision of the whole Railway Act, and this period of the session, when we are nearing its end, does not seem to me the proper time to take up so important a matter. But in the meantime I would ask the Minister of Justice to refer a case to the Supreme Court so that we might get the opinion of that court as to whether the legislation proposed is ultra vires or within our jurisdiction. The importance of this matter demands that some such reference should be made. I do not agree with some gentlemen who have spoken this afternoon, that because certain legislation might be within our jurisdiction, we ought to pass it and then let those who challenge our jurisdiction make good their claim. That, it seems to me, would be an unwise policy. A mistake on our part might involve the country in serious damages. We have had already to pay hundreds of thous-Mr. HACKETT.
ands of dollars in consequence of legislating beyond our jurisdiction. Before we pass legislation, let us be sure that we have the light to do so, and not force private individuals to contest our right and perhaps be subjected to a defeat in the courts with all the consequences of a defeat of that nature. Just one word with reference to the express business of the Intercolonial. I cannot agree with my hon. friend the Minister of Railways that because the Dominion Express Company has a monopoly in some parts of Canada, we should not allow it to break the monopoly on the Intercolonial. Between certain points of the Intercolonial, for instance between Levis and Moncton, the Canadian Express Company has a monopoly. Between Truro and Sydney in the eastern part of Nova Scotia, on the island of Cape Breton, the Canadian Express Company also enjoys a monopoly, and it has likewise a monopoly on the short line between Oxford and Pictou. In view of the demands made by the people for better regulations and rates, it seems to me the Minister of Railways should seriously consider the giving to the Dominion Express Company equal rights on the government railways with the Canadian Express Company. As regards the question of government ownership of express companies, it is one which we should take considerable time to consider. There are difficulties that at once suggest themselves. It would necessitate the government becoming the owner of horses, carriages, harness and the general equipment of an express company.
How does the government handle the mails ?

By tender and contract, and you could not very well handle the express business in that way. However, I have not given the question sufficient study and consideration to be in a position to express a decided opinion, but considering the facts, I can see no objection to granting to the Dominion Express Company, equal privileges on the government roads with the Canadian Express Company, especially as that would be nothing more than fair to the people of the maritime provinces. In the meantime I trust my hon. friend the Minister of Justice will see his way clear to have the question of jurisdiction referred to the Supreme Court for an opinion.

Has the hon. gentleman any documentary evidence to show that we are nearing the end of the session ? If so, will he kindly lay it on the table ?
SMr. GOURLEY. I want to say to the hon. Minister of Railways that I believe public opinion in the maritime provinces is in favour of free trade in express companies. The legal difficulty I know nothing about at present, but there should be some way of getting around it. We want active competi-

tion in express companies on the Intercolonial, and there is a feeling among the people that they are unjustly treated by having one company given vested rights in the government railway to the exclusion of others. The people of course have to suffer the consequences of want of competition. I would support my hon. friend the Minister of Railways in any fair measure ip which he would give free trade to express companies.
