Mr. MACLEAN moved to amend the Bill by'adding a section which will read as follows :
Section io of the said Act is amended by striking out the words ' and his opinion on any question which, in the opinion of the commissioners, is a question of law shall prevail.
He said : This is to remove a difficulty which has arisen in connection with the Railway Commission and which came to the front not long ago. The towns of Port Arthur and Port William have a municipal telephone service. After a great deal of trouble a year ago we got a clause put in the Railway Act to the effect that every railway company is bound, on the order of the Railway Commission, to give access to any municipal or incorporated telephone system that seeks admission to the stations of any railway company. I secured that amendment by repeated argument last session and pointing out that the Canadian Pacific Railway had refused access to its station to independent companies on the plea that it had made a contract-this old nlea of a contract-with the Bell Telephone Company allowing that company and no other telephone company to have connection with their station. Parliament was good enough after a severe fight to put a clause in the Act to this effect:
Whenever any municipality or corporation has authority to construct, operate and maintain a telephonic system in any district, and is desirous of obtaining telephonic connection or communication with or within any station or premises of the company, in such district and cannot .agreej with thei company with respect thereto, such municipality or corporation may apply to the board for leave therefor, and the board may order the company to provide for such connection or communication upon such terms as to compensation as the board deems just and expedient, and may order and direct how, when, where, by whom and upon what terms and conditions such telephonic connection or communication shall be constructed, operated and maintained.
Hon. Mr. Blair, who was then Minister of Railways and Canals and who piloted this Bill through parliament, told the House that this Bill is to meet the emergency which' I have stated and to remove the grievances of the people who own independent telephone lines, the grievances of Locust Hill,
Port Arthur, Fort William, and other places. With that understanding I accepted that amendment. Time passed and the commission was organized. Hon. Mr. Blair became chairman of the commission. These people of Port Arthur and Fort William, Locust Hill and other places appeared before the commission and asked that the railway should be compelled to allow them telephonic access to the station. The case was argued and the, permission given. The majority of the commission of three members -Hon. Mr. Blair, ex-Minister of Railways ; Hon. Mr. Bernier, ex-Minister of Inland Revenue, and Professor Mills, who - had been selected on account of his business capacity, I believe-ruled that under this clause these local telephone companies had the right of access to these stations under the provisions of the Act. But the chairman of the commission, Mr. Blair, said : You may be in favour of giving these telephone companies access to the station, but there is another clause in the Act which makes this a legal issue and so brings it wholly and solely within my jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Section 10.

That is section 10, which reads as follows :
Not less than two commissioners shall attend at the hearing of every case, and the chief commissioner, when present, shall preside, and his opinion upon any question, which in the opinion of the commissioners is a question of law, shall prevail.
Now, if there was any justification for the Bill passed last session establishing a railway commission it was that the people of Canada were at last to have a tribunal that would control these railway companies and regulate their charges, and this would be done by business men in a business way, without the long-drawn-out system of the courts. It is on that ground that hon. gentlemen opposite are justifying the Railway Act before the public. They make it their boast that at last they have established a tribunal that will deal with these questions speedily. But," instead of having such a tribunal it now turns out that it is to all intents and purposes a court of law, and that the chief justice of that court is supreme and can override his two colleagues. And to show that I do not go outside the record, let me read a few lines from what Mr. Blair said. This is in a despatch dated Ottawa, March 22nd, and gives an account of the speech made by Mr. Blair at the opening of the Railway Commission :
I think I can say for the board-I certainly say it for myself as being responsible for the legal conclusions that may be arrived at.
So, he has the right to say what is the legal issue and to tell his colleagues to sit aside. . Never was such a lecture delivered in any legal tribunal before as that given by Mr. Blair to his colleagues. In effect he

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
said :	Now, you two get off the bench ; I
will occupy it myself : this is a question of law and I will decide it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: From what section of the law is that quoted ?

That is the substance of what Mr. Blair told these good little boys who had been sent to accompany him. He told them to sit down and he would interpret the law. And his interpretation is to the effect that the people of Port Arthur and Fort William, and the farmers of Locust Hill, and the local companies in Quebec and the Northwest, who want telephonic connection with these stations, can only have it by paying enormous damages to the Bell Telephone Company. That is the sum and substance of his decision. That is the barren verdict given the people by the chairman of the Railway Commission. But we propose that this Samson shall be shorn of his locks, that he shall be made only co-equal with his colleagues and that all three members of the commission shall be judges of the law as they are judges of the facts. I do not believe in putting the great commercial interests of this country absolutely in the hands of a lawyer. In many cases under our law we summoiT a jury and the jury becomes the judge of both law and fact. That is the system that should be followed in this case. The business men and farmers of this country do not want to be left at the mercy of a lawyer at the head of this court.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: There is the right to appeal, is there not ?

He says there is the right to appeal to the Privy Council and the Supreme Court, and these people have been sent there. They came down the other day to make some motion in regard to it and they were told that the commission was going west and it would take a long w7hile to get into the Supreme Court. And the chairman of the commission is on record as saying in effect : You had better not go to the Privy Council. He warned them not to go.
Some bon. MEMBERS. Oh, oh.
Mr. Blair is a good lawyer, and

This is what he said :
I think that an appeal to the Governor in Council would, not be desirable in that case. It is a question of law purely and simply so far as it now stands. And-I say it with all respect-the Governor in Council is not a tribunal to determine questions of law.
When the hon. gentleman speaks of the Privy Council he does not refer to the judicial committee of the Privy Council ?

No. This is the position taken by this new Czar. He says, in Mr. MACLEAN.
effect :	My colleagues' opinion does not
count when it is a matter of law7, and I do not think that you litigants should go to the Privy Council, though you have a right to go. The people of this country do not ivant law, they want service, they want the simple, common right to put their telephone lines into the station of these great railway corporations that they have created. And, as I said before, who are the people who ask for this accommodation-it can be called accommodation-for the railways ? " They are the clients of the railway companies. All that they want access to the railway station for is to be able to ask if their freight has arrived, if the train is on time, when they should send goods to the station for shipment, and so on. They are all anxious to do business with these railways and they find that this Bell Telephone Company, by a contract, has got between them and' the railways and they cannot get into .these railway stations.
It,is the Grand Trunk Railway of Canada to whom w7e are giving $150,000,000 to build a transcontinental railway that we propose to empower to enslave the'people ; it is the Canadian Pacific Railway to whom we have given millions and millions of dollars, and to whom we propose further to give power to enslave the people by preventing them from having telephone access to railway stations. I believe that the contract by which this railway company contracted to keep rival companies out of their stations is bad in law', I believe it is against the public interest, and would so be declared by the courts if appealed to. Therefore under these circumstances I come here with this little amendment asking parliament to change the law so that the supreme jurisdiction now vested in the Chairman of the Railway Commission may be taken awTay, and that the questions w'hich come before him may be tried, both as questions of business and as questions of law7, by some other men, by tw7o lawyers if you will. You may not have two, but don't make monkeys of the colleagues of the chairman. Both of these men were seized of this case, both of them gave excellent judgments. I have asked the Minister of Justice to read the judgments that were given by the Hon. Mr.. Bernier and Professor Mills. They are both sound, practical judgments that appeal to every one. They said : These people are entitled to go into these railway stations under this Act, and we make the order forthwith. But the Czar stands up and says : You shall not do so, this is a question of law7, and I take it out of your hands. So the people are denied this privilege of going into railway stations.
The commissioners must agree that it is a question of law, then the chairman has power to decide.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not find the word ' Czar ' defined in the Act.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: No, but here is what he does find. In a statement given out by the Chairman of the Committee on March 22 last, Mr. Blair, the Chairman, said : ' I certainly say it as being responsible for the legal conclusions that may be arrived at.'

But we have section 10 of the statute and here is what it says :
Not less than two commissioners shall attend at the hearing of every case, and the chief commissioner, when present, shall preside, and his opinion upon any question, which in the opinion of the commissioners is a question of law, shall prevail.

I know that is the case, find it was on the strength of this that he immediately acts without these two men. But of course they should have stood out and asserted themselves. The defence that will be offered here to-day will probably be that there should be no such clause as that in the Act. Take that out and let us make these two men co-equal. Do that, and I believe that the business men, the farmers of this country will have some confidence in these men who will proceed to grant relief in many cases.

Is it not a fact that about seven-tenths of all the cases that come before that commission involve questions of law ? A man's right is generally determined by his legal right. It is true that he may have a moral right, but if a man has a legal right and one that can be fairly defended in law, it gives him a different status from that he would otherwise occupy. In nearly all these cases there is a question of law involved, and if questions of law can be decided by the chairman, surely the other two commissioners might as well stay at home. We know that when the Railway Commission was contemplated at first, it was contended strongly that it should consist of three men, one a lawyer, one a railway expert, and one a man who should be a man of common sense, a man who would be versed generally in matters of trade and commerce. It was set forth that it was essentially requisite to have a commission composed in that way so that they might bring their varied intelligences to bear on the different questions that would come before them. It was never contended that the legal mind on that commission should control the others on any question, whether of law or of fact.

I think the position is this : This commission must necessarily have a lawyer among its members. Whatever government appoints these commissioners will endeavour to get the best men obtainable. The salaries paid them are probably based on that principle. I do not think any one will dispute the ability of the present Chairman of the Commission, as a lawyer. It was to be expected that we should find such a section as section 10 in 214

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: this Act. Necessarily, as my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has pointed out, questions of law enter into nearly every dispute that will come before the commission. Now a layman, be he ever so clever, be he ever so good a business man, be he ever so well versed in railway matters, is not as competent to judge of the legal effect of an argument, or of an existing condition, as is a trained legal mind. Therefore, it is only reasonable to expect that when the commission has to decide upon a question where a legal point is involved, the decision on that legal point belongs and should be vested in that member of the commission who is a legal gentleman, in the present case in the chairman. Now they have got to agree, and it is by virtue of section 10 that they have first to agree that there is a legal point involved. Then which of the members of that commission, the trained legal mind on the one hand, or the member who may have no legal knowledge whatever, is the better judge of the question of law, or the better able to decide what law should apply to the point in dispute ? That is altogether outside the numerous questions or circumstances that may arise that are not of a legal character.

Will the hon. gentleman pardon me a moment ? Are not these colleagues of the chairman who are constantly engaged in construing the various clauses in the Act, by that fact qualified to engage in the business of interpreting the law ?

That does not affect my argument at all ; they may or may not be so. The other two commissioners, no matter how able they may be in every respect from a business point of view, in their commercial knowledge, in their technical railway knowledge, or in their general intelligence, are not as capable of construing a legal point as is a trained legal mind. But we do not rest there. There is an appeal. The Hon. Mr. Blair, Chairman of the Commission, in the case mentioned, says there is an appeal, if I remember correctly, even to the Privy Council. These parties have their right of appeal, first it is to the government. Then there is a section which specially provides that either party to a dispute may, on his own motion, and upon giving such security as directed by statute, ask for the opinion of the Supreme Court of Canada upon any question which, in the opinion of the board, is a question of law. A reference can be made at the request of the Governor in Council. Either party may do so, or the board may do so. Surely that is all the protection any one wants. You may say that the board won't do it because they won't stultify themselves. Then it is open to you, the privilege is granted to you. But at all events, I think that meets one of the objections raised by my hon. friend. It: is not as if the Chairman of the Railway

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: Commission was the Czar in the matter, and his decision was final in all cases, because it is not.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: As far as all matters which do not involve some question of -law are concerned, the majority of the board must determine them. As far as questions of Jaw are concerned, they will eventually have to be decided by some person. If the board should proceed without regard to the statute under which it is acting, and by which it is controlled, of course there would be a remedy outside, because its acts would be beyond its jurisdiction and inoperative, and would be so declared by the courts. If the chairman of the Railway Commission could himself decide that a particular matter is a question of law, and therefore arrogate to himself everything that came before the board, there would be good ground for making some alteration in the law, but the point that has been more particularly urged by my hon. friend from East York is that the other two members of the board were rather weak in yielding when they should not have yielded. That is not due to a defect in the law, but it is due to a defect in the constitution of the board.
No ; it is due to the bulldosing of the chief, who says :	I am responsible for the legal conclusion.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In the ultimate view if would be due to the weakness of the -gentlemen who did not assert themselves as members of the commission in the way they were entitled to do under the law. I think this court ought to be a speedy court, but at the same time when the court has to consider legal questions, it must have regard to legal principles, and it must be bound by the terms of the statute which it has to consider and by the law under which it is acting. Under these circumstances, it would appear to me to be a little dangerous to remove this provision from the statute until we have had a little more experience and until we have found some real injustice resulting from it, because the injustice which is said to have resulted does not seem to be due to anything in the Act, but rather to the fault of the two junior members of the board, who did not take the position which they should have taken.
I would like to ask my hon. friend the leader of the opposition and also my hon. friend the Minister of Rail ways and 'Canals whether they know of any other court in the world so constituted ?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes.
What court ?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
In the ordinary courts of the country, where the jury determines questions of fact, -the judge always determines questions of law. The jury are the absolute judges of the facts. They can determine the question of fact against the Mr. GALLIHER.
charge of the judge, but when it comes to a question of law, the judge must determine that, subject to the same appeal as that which is created by this statute.

The case is not apposite. What I want to know is where you will find a court in which the chairman of the court says to his colleagues : This is a question for me to determine, not you. Take the case of the Interstate Commerce Commission in the United States, which is dealing with similar matters, and which was appointed for the very same purpose ; do you mean to tell me that the chairman of that commission has any more power than his colleagues have ? We all know about the judge and jury, and 1 admitted that some time ago, but here is a commission appointed by parliament at the request of the people of this country, of the merchants and the farmers, to deal with these ques tions and to deal with them speedily. Now we are told that these questions are practically all questions of law, and the Chairman arrogates to himself the decision of these questions of law. We are getting back to the old thing. Everybody who is a lawyer in this House is getting up and saying that there is a legal obstruction in the way. It is always -a case of contract. Somebody must interpret contracts, and now we have the railway companies contracting themselves out in connection with express companies, we have the railway companies contracting themselves out in connection with the telephone companies, and when the people come here for relief we find the lawyers one after another getting up and saying : This is a question of law, it has to be taken into the courts and there has to be litigation.
Mr. iSCOTT. Would passenger rates be a question of law ?
No ; of justice.

But you have no confidence in the commission now.
Mr. MAC-LEAN. I will come to that. I want to tell my hon. friend that there are a good many people in the Northwest Territories who want to -have telephone communication with the railway stations there. The farmers want to have it, and the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver),, if he were in his place, as he ought to be, to back up what he said the other day, would be helping me to -fight this battle against this -frightful monopoly of the Bell Telephone Company -and that great railway company cut there, who are trying to perpetrate an injustice upon the people. The people of the Northwest -are pretty tired of the present conditions, they want telephone communication with the railway stations in the west, and, while, they are anxious to secure it, the Bell Telephone Company are busy every day building lines, getting into possession and placing themselves in a position to prevent any independent company from

gaining access to the railway stations. Down in the province of Quebec, according to the statement of a gentleman who came to see me the other evening, they are building hundreds of miles of independent lines, but the one thing that blocks them is the contract between the Bell Telephone Company and the railway companies, and the one thing that justifies this contract is the clause in the Railway Act which allows the chairman of the commission to take the position he is taking, when he claims that this is a matter of law and that his colleagues are not judges of the law. After his colleagues had considered this case and had said that these independent telephone companies were entitled to enter these stations, they turned around, for what reason 1 do not know, and allowed the chairman of the commission to arrogate to himself the decision of the case. If there had been a genuine farmer on the commission, as the right lion. Prime Minister promised there would be, he would not have consented to have had it interpreted as a question of law. But the chairman of the commission said that it was a question of law, and there it remains. It is now in the courts ; go there ; go to this court; go to some other court ; make it a legal question ; talk about contracts ; talk about the constitution, but all the time humbug the people and give no relief ! It is relief that is wanted. This commission is one that should afford relief. If there is a grievance, and this country has a fair grievance in this matter, there should be a tribunal to remedy that grievance, and in the old days the public men found a remedy for public grievances. They had that remedy in the voting of supplies, but in some way things have changed now, all kinds of public grievances are permitted, and the duty devolves upon two or three men to make the fight in this parliament for public rights. Sometimes I have to carry it on, sometimes other men have to carry it on, and it is carried on as well as it can be, but it has come to this that supplies are voted while these public grievances continue. 'Hon. gentlemen in this House pledged themselves on the platform all over the country that, as Liberals, they were the friends of the people, and that they believed in constitutional progress, but they forget that constitutional progress in Canada has consisted in the remedy of the grievances of the people. I am sorry to say there is no effort being made now to remedy these grievances in connection with the voting of supplies. We are voting supplies, we are paying salaries to this commission, $10,000 to one and $8,000 to two others, with a company of clerks and servitors of one kind and another added, and they are doing nothing to remedy these grievances but giving the public a lawsuit. Go to another court ' We did not create this court, we did not put this country to this great expense, we did not find these places 214$
for public servants, to be told,' when we bring a grievance before it, that it is a matter of law, and that we must go from one court to another. If that is to be the answer, all well and good ; the public have to be met, and the public have to be met by hon. gentlemen who sit in this House. The public will be seized of this question, they are being seized of it, and they expect different answers from legal quibbles and contentions to the effect that you must go from court to court, and that no remedy is to be given.

The hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) is not quite consistent in the argument which he makes. If I understand his amendment rightly, it is only an amendment to section 10 of the Railway Act, which says that when, in the opinion of the chairman of the commission, it is a question of law, the decision of that question must be left to the chairman-of the commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: ' When in the opinion of the board.'

Of the commissioners, yes. My hon. friend says that you should not force people who go before this court to go before another court, but his amendment does not go far enough to secure that end. What does he want ? He wants this commission to decide on questions of law, he wants this commission, which is composed of one lawyer and as the case is now, one notary public, and another gentleman of no legal attainments to decide between railway companies and persons who go before this commission, sometimes in cases involving questions of liability and enormous amounts of money without any appeal to a higher court. I would put this question to any reasonable man and would be willing to discuss it before an assembly of reasonable men and ask them if they would submit to the danger of being judged in the last resort by this commission.
I do not propose to refuse an appeal.

If my hon. friend does not propose to abolish the appeal granted in section 43, his amendment falls short of the argument he has just given. The whole argument of my hon. friend was that you must give the people of this country a tribunal of last resort before which they can go and not send litigants from one court to the other. His amendment then falls short of this argument ; he does not propose to amend section 43 which gives the right of appeal. Now, I ask. what will be the ultimate result of the amendment which he proposes ? Supposing that the majority of the commissioners decide a question of law. Does my hon. friend think that even if two commissioners were of the opinion that

they should reverse the opinion of the chief commissioner on a question of law that the railway company interested or the other party iitigating, if it was an important case, would not go further and take an appeal V Does my hon. friend think that for a moment ?
No.

Then I say his amendment does not go far enough if lie is really sincere in his desire to attain this object. He should go a step further but if he goes that step further he is trying to legislate not. only against the interests of the railway companies who have to go before the Railway Commission, but also against the interests of any litigant whose case comes before the gentlemen for adjudication. It is no use making speeches to the effect that this is a cheap tribunal before which the people can go. a tribunal which would decide in the last resort so that they would not have to go from court to court. Unless he proposes also to abrogate section 43 of the Railway Act, which gives the right of appeal. I again repeat that even if two commissioners were of a different opinion on a question of law from the chief commissioner, an appeal would still be taken, and the public would not have the cheap court of which my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) speaks.

To supplement what my hon. friend from Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) has said I would like to draw the attention of the hon. gentleman who moved the amendment. (Mr. Maclean) to the fact that the system we have here is the same as that which prevails in England. My hon. friend is aware that in England there are live railway commissioners, two appointed and three ex officio. There is one ex officio member for England one for Ireland and one for Scotland. Three commissioners constitute a quorum of the five, but one ex officio commissioner must always sit and he must always be a judge appointed by, the Chancellor in England or the Chief Justice in Ireland, or the Chief Legal Authority in Scotland and the chairman we have here is, as in England, always a judge.
In the definition of his jurisdiction is it set forth that he is the judge of the law ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That goes as a mere matter of common sense. There you have three commissioners two of whom are laymen and one a judge. Invariably in a commission of that kind the judge's opinion would prevail on a question of law.
Not necessarily.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend is too good a logician not to see that it would be absurd that on a question of law two laymen would decide as against a trained legal gentleman put there practically to
decide legal questions. My hon. friend sees how absurd that would be.
No he does not ; he sees the quibble.
This discussion is valuable as giving to us some idea of the Railway Act. The difficulty which I think my learned friend-

Pardon me, I do not want the honour.
Mr. GOURLEY-that the hon. member for East York has is with these two farmer members of the commission. He asks that we should have at least three farmers but the difficulty is that with the two farmers they would first have to agree that it was a question of law before the legal man has any right to say a word. Therefore it shows me that farmers are very poor men to put upon a court.
But there is no farmer on it.

You are speaking of farmers' decisions and I assume that these two gentlemen who are not lawyers would give farmers' decisions. The remedy for my hon. friend's difficulty is to have two other lawyers, and I would suggest that he move that the two farmers be struck off and two more lawyers be put on.
I do not agree there.
And then you would get justice.
You would get plenty of law.

I am bound to say after considerable experience, and the committee will agree with me that I do not promote the interests of my trade very much,' that three lawyers on a commission would give more justice in half an hour, than a dozen farmers would in a thousand years.
I do not object, provided the three are co-equal.

A lawyer goes at a thing right ; he looks at it from all sides, he sums up and does justice. I am surprised that we have not three trained men on this commission, because the commissioners are constantly dealing, under this Act. with vested interests, with rights of property, and I cannot imagine how a man would protect these rights of property unless he had legal training.
Do you think that with more than one legal gentleman on the board they would ever agree ?

They would never disagree. They might start to disagree in the morning but they would agree at noon, or if they did not agree at noon, they would

agree at night. A good lawyer has no pride of opinion. I may have a strong opinion now, hut I may change it at once and within the next hour' I may change it again. The only thing about which a lawyer is anxious is that the sun shall not go down upon him having a wrong opinion. He may change his opinion a thousand times a day. but will never let the sun go down upon him holding a wrong opinion if he can help it. A layman on the other hand may have a wrong opinion in the morning but through pride, conceit and personal bullheadedness will hold to that opinion be he right or wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He does not care about the sun going down.

He does not care about the sun going down upon his wrong opinion. With regard to Mr. Blair I may say that when I first entered this House I was rather prejudiced against him, coming from the maritime provinces, being a Tory and not having personal acquaintance with him ; but after being here for two or three years I learned to have for him a great admiration. He was strong and clear, always understood the facts and had a firm grip of the whole circumstances of any case under consideration. If there is any man in Canada who should have the right of settling these matters and should have the confidence of the people in doing so, he is that man. I have a kind of sympathy for my hon. friend here (Mr. Maclean). There should be three farmers on this commission, or three lawyers. The great thing is not to mix up good material like a lawyer with alloy like farmers. You will always have a base metal when you mix gold with bronze ; you will always have difficulties with a mixed tribunal. I think my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) should amend his Bill so as to have either three lawyers or three farmers.
Mr. WILLIAM ROSS (Yictoriai. I am sorry that the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Gourley) has such a poor opinion of laymen generally.
No, I have a very high 'opinion.
Of farmers. It is not long since I heard him saying that every elector in Colchester was equal, if not superior to everybody in this House.
More than equal, I say.

I did not al-togther agree with him at that time, and I do not agree with him now. I think there are plenty of farmers in the country who are quite as capable of judging the merits of n case if it does not become a question of law as any lawyer in this House. I do not want to discredit the ability of lawyers in their
profession, and it is almost charming to see how they a'gree in this instance, because the Act gives them greater power than they had before. They always want to climb up and get more influence by Act of parliament than they had before. That is generally the aim of lawyers. I have expressed my opinion in this House of the chairman of that committee before, and I have not changed it since. I am not going to repeat it now ; but I would not withdraw to-day a single word that I said about that gentleman at the time he tendered his resignation:

I am sorry to see that the weight of legal argument this afternoon is so strongly against the hon. member for East York, because behind all this there is this fact, that the intention of parliament as expressed last year has been absolutely frustrated, in conpection with giving rights to independent telephone companies to connect with railway stations. When the Bill was up here last year, and even before, the towns of Fort William and Port Arthur were very prominently before the members of the House and the country with their grievance against the Bell Telephone Company. They had a municipal system of telephones, which was refused connection with the railway stations in those two towns. While we were discussing the matter, the mayor and councils of those two towns came down here and put their position before the Railway Committee. The Minister of Railways was altogether opposed to the Bell Telephone Company being interfere^ with in their monopoly in the railway stations of the country. After the matter had been thoroughly discussed both here and in the Railway Committee, the minister became aware that the opinion on both sides of the House was overwhelmingly against him, and he finally brought in an amendment to meet their wishes. The amendment was thought by the minister himself and the members of the House to give independent companies the right to put their instruments in the stations of the railway companies, and the clause passed in that way. We did not know then that the Minister of Railways of last session was to be the chairman of the Railway Com mission, this year ; but so it happened, and this very clause was the first important one to come before the commission. The result, whether right or wrong, was to completely frustrate the intention of the majority of the members of this House last year. Now. something should be done to put us in the position which we thought we occupied. Perhaps the hon. piember for East York is wrong in proposing to strike out this part of this section. Perhaps he ought to have taken another section. At all events, some proposition should be brought forward under this Bill to put us in the position which -we thought we were in with respect to independent telephones last year.

Just a word. I understood that this Railway Commission was to decide all questions between the railway companies, the farmers, the travelling public, and every one concerned. I had no idea that we were to have a one-man power on that commission ; but it seems that is what it is down to. Then we might as well save the expense of the other two, and allow the one-man, if he must have a legally trained mind, to decide all questions. The other two men might as well be dispensed with. The first thing we want to know in regard to this matter is, what is law ? I, always understood law was common sense. Some of the greatest minds in Britain that the world ever saw knew nothing about law ; they were not trained in law. Men may have great minds and never study law. I do not think we are obliged to fall back on a man who has been to college and studied and learned to quibble on words-because that is what lawyers generally do. What we want are facts-whatever is true and right. Whom do we find getting up and defending the Czar of the commission ? Every lawyer in the House, while the farmers are ignored. If the amendment of the hon. member for East York is not made, we shall have trouble of this kind every year. We had better settle it now for all time, that whatever that committee decides to do shall be the law in this matter.

I regret that there has been only a farmer on this side of the House to take the side of the farmers in this issue. The farmers all over this country are asking for this relief. They are simply asking that these railway companies, who are enjoying immense subsidies of the people's money, shall allow the people's telephone lines, which are struggling against a great monopoly, to have access to these railway stations to do business with them.
J believe that under the common law of this country, that contract is against the public * interest of this country, and is illegal ; I believe these railway companies could be compelled, irrespective of the railway commission to give that access; but as it is they are denying it. The farmers are refused this relief, and there is not a farmer on the other side of the House to get up and say a word for them. The Postmaster General, who used to make my own province ring with the complaint that in this matter the farmers were being bled white, is not in his place ; hon. gentlemen who represent the farmers have not a word to say in their interest; and the men from the Northwest who are threatened with this Bell monopoly, have not a word to say, although if a decision were given in the Port Arthur case, the matter would be settled in all parts of the country.

The decision was given on March 22. Representatives of the town of Port Arthur came to Toronto. I had an interview with the mayor and several representatives of the two towns. They said they were on their way to Ottawa, and they had incurred great expense to have the case argued, but they did not want more litigation. They wanted relief first of all. If we cannot get it in this way, I have another amendment to meet the case which may command the support of my hon. friend from Montmorency. They sent an agent here the other day to get an appointment for them, and they were told the old story, that the commissioners were going to the coast, that they would be back some time in September, and that they would then make a reference to the Supreme Court.

Between the month of March and now there must have been time for them to have lodged an appeal. If the decision was really not right and there was an injustice done, they surely would have had time to put in an appeal and have it decided.

And the matter would have gone to the Supreme Court. The chairman of the commission was good enough to say he would make a reference to the Supreme Court. That court would probably construe it to be a question of law, and these farmers would have had to pay enormous damages to the Bell Telephone Company in order to have this telephone connection.

Supposing section 10 did not exist at all and the chief commissioner would not have the decision on a question of law, and suppose the three commissioners decided against the telephone company, does the hon. gentleman not think that, under section 43, there would have been an appeal by the company against that decision ?
I grant that.
Then your amendment does not meet the case.
It is a bastard court which gives one man more power than his colleagues.
Order.
That is a good English word.
But not used in good English society.

Yes, I am not using it in any wrong sense. It is a very fitting word to describe a court in which one judge decides everything and tells the others to

sit down. The jurisdiction should be coequal. I am willing to accept the suggestion made that the three judges should be lawyers, but at any rate they should have equal powers. The questions that come before them are almost altogether questions of fact. They are such questions as ordinary business men can decide just as we decide them in this House. Why' must the judge of necessity be a lawyer if the man who makes the law is not a lawyer ?
That makes the necessity greater.

An ordinary man has the right to assist in making the law, but once it is made, we are told that it must be interpreted by legal men. I object to that. The ordinary business men of the country could very well decide these questions. Such men to decide them across the line, where they have an Interstate Commission, and where substantial relief is given the public by the decisions of that commission.

I wish to express myself in favour of some change in the law so that the different telephone companies in Canada shall have the right to connect with the larger corporations. I had a conversation with a leading business man of the town of Port Arthur the other day, and he told me that the telephone system between Port Arthur and Fort William was a perfect success. The business men of both places were well, satisfied with the local service, but they had a strong complaint that they were unable to get outside connections with the Bell Telephone. I do not think that parliament should pass any legislation which would interfere with the rights of the Bell Telephone Company. That company has done very much for the people. It has done good service in many cases.
They make you pay for it.

I do not think this constitutes any very great grievance, but I do not think it is in the interests of the people that one or more than one very large corporation should have the monopoly of sending messages to different parts of Canada. If a local company -s established in any locality, it should have the right to connect with the long distance telephone service, 'so long as it is willing to pay. I am in favour of legislation which will allow the different local companies to connect with the larger telephone companies and thus have the privilege of sending messages to different parts of Canada. We must bear in mind that the telephone is an increasing business. Men who years ago never went near a telephone office are now its daily visitors, and a considerable portion of the business of the country is transacted by telephone. This is the case, not only with banking and commercial institutions, but with farmers. Parliament should therefore provide such legislation as will give local telephone companies access to the long distance service, provided they are willing to pay a reasonable rate.

I have always held the view that when we incorporate a railway company we bring it under the Railway Act, and that the Act contemplates that every part of the public should have equal rights in doing business with the railways.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is right.

In this case a patron of the Bell Telephone Company has the advantage of enjoying conveniences which are denied other men who want to do business with it. That is not equal rights to all. It is discrimination in favour of one as against another, and the law does not contemplate any such discrimination. We are told over and over again that when we give railway corporations the right to build railways, they become common carriers and must treat all alike, but the Bell Telephone Company are doing just the opposite and we are supporting them. It should be the duty of parliament to break down that injustice and put all on an equal footing. If a railway company is to be allowed to give the Bell Telephone Company a monopoly in its stations, all those who are not patrons of that company are discriminated against. It may be that the law as it stands would justify the Bell Company, but that certainly never was the intention of parliament. Parliament has declared over and over again that its intention was that railway corporations shall* treat all alike ; and if the law enables them to avoid that obligation, this parliament should amend it, and if parliament fails to do its duty, the people will have a just complaint against the government of the day and those members who refused to secure to the public equal rights. If this be allowed, you can take any part of the country you like, and for one who will enjoy the privilege you will find fifteen or twenty denied it. That is not meting out equal treatment to all.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Lest I should be misunderstood in anything I have said, I desire to explain that the amendment I was considering was simply this-to strike out from this section the words ' and his opinion on any question which, in the opinion of the commissioners, is a question of law, should prevail.' The point which has been discussed by the last two hon. gentlemen who have spoken is one which arises more particularly on the next amendment. I was expressing no opinion on that. The only thing I desire to point out is that the question of law must be decided by a tribunal

of some kind which is supposed to possess the knowledge requisite for the construing of statutes. My hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) argues that the chief commissioner should not have that power, being a lawyer. Of course, I am disposed to give every possible weight to everything the hon. gentleman urges in that regard. But the case that has been brought forward as an illustration is one which, whatever might be done with this amendment, would, in the end, be decided by the Supreme Court, it seems to me. Under the law as it stands, the chief commissioner has decided a point of law. An appeal lies to the Supreme Court. If it were otherwise, if the two gentlemen not members of the legal profession had decided this case in the opposite way and had overruled the opinion of the legal member of the board, undoubtedly the board as a whole would permit an appeal to the Supreme Court. So, in the end the Supreme Court would decide the question of law. That is altogether apart from the merits of the question whether or not the decision of the chief commissioner was right. If it was right the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) proposes to so alter the law that the decisions hereafter shall be otherwise. In that connection we must consider the justice of the decision pronounced by the chief commissioner. Upon this amendment. I am not expressing any opinion upon the desirability of altering that law in that regard. When we come to consider that amendment I shall be prepared to express an opinion. I desire to make it clear that I have not said anything that can be construed as opposed to the amendment which we shall be called upon to discuss ^In a little while.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: When we do come to the discussion of the next amendment of which my hon. friend Air. Maclean) has given notice, I shall have an opportunity to show that the statement made as to the effect of the judgment rendered in the Port Arthur case is incorrect. Because, one commissioner did not overrule two. The hon. gentleman will see, if he considers the effect of the judgment, that the chief commissioner and Hon. Mr. Bernier are, in effect agreed, and that the dissent is on the part of Mr. Mills. However, we will deal with that on the next question.

My position is that when a court is established its members should have equal jurisdiction, power and weight ; that one ought not to be superior to the others. And I still stick to that. I propose to do away with all distinctions in the court In this respect. All I want is a court constituted of men of authority in deciding all matters that come before them. I think that is a good rule and it has never been departed from in auy case that I know of. Certainly no instance put forward here todays shows a tribunal composed of men of 1 Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
unequal power, one being given the authority to overrule the others.
