Section 193 of the said Act is amended by adding the following words :-' And such compensation shall be limited to the direct and immediate local damages actually suffered by reason of such construction, operation and maintenance by the railway company at such station or premises, and not from any cause, matter or business extending beyond the same.'
He said :	This amendment is to meet
the case of Port Arthur and Fort William. The object is to provide that independent telephone companies shall have the right of access to these stations and that the only damage they shall pay is the actual damage incurred by the intrusion-that they shall not pay any damage that the Bell Telephone Company or the railway company may plead that they have sustained under any contract. The clause was drawn by some legal gentlemen who are interested in the Port Arthur decision. If the point were made clear, as I believe it will * be by this amendment, there could be no such decision

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) has the decision, would he be good enough to explain it for the benefit of some of us who are not as familiar with the case as he is ?

I am sorry to say that I have mislaid the decision. But the substance of it, as I understand it, was that these independent companies would have to go to court to have it decided whether they should not pay large damages to both the telephone and the railway company. The Canadian Pacific Railway and Bell Telephone Company pleaded before the Railway Commission that this right of access meant hundreds of thousands of dollars of damage to them.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: How could they plead that ?

The contract between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Bell Telephone Company provides that, in consideration of the Bell Telephone Company being granted a monopoly in the Canadian Pacific Railway stations, the Canadian Pacific Railway shall be supplied free with all the telephone instruments needed in connection with their business. I have read the contract in this House, and it is on record in ' Hansard.' The Grand Trunk has a similar contract with the Bell Telephone Company. Hon. gentlemen ought to read the equipment called for even in the city of Montreal in the way of free telephones. There can be no doubt that, if independent telephone companies were allowed access to the railway stations, the loss to these other

concerns would be very considerable. But to avoid that being cminted as damages against the independent companies, this amendment has been drawn. Under it these companies can plead only the actual damages incurred by the intrusion of the wires into the railway station.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It might be of some use to the committee for me to state the circumstances of the reference to the Railway Commissioners arising out of the Port Arthur and Fort William case. These two municipalities, the town of Port Arthur and the town of Fort William, owned and operated a telephone system within the limits of the two towns. They applied to the board of Railway Commissioners, under section 193 of the Railway Act, for an order as follows :
Directing the railway company to allow the installation of telephone instruments In the railway stations of the Canadian Pacific Railway and for leave to connect the same with their telephone system.
That is to say, for leave to connect the station with the telephone system with the town of Port Arthur with the telephone system of the company. Now prior to the enactment of this section 193
Has the Canadian Pacific a telephone system in connection with their railway ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: A telephone system in the station.
But it is only to connect with that system, it is only to get access to the station.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Prior to the enactment of section 193, in May, 1902. an agreement was made between the railway and the Bell Telephone whereby the latter company for valuable consideration, had granted for a period of ten years, the exclusive privilege of placing telephone instruments, apparatus and wires in the several stations, offices and premises of the railway in Canada where the telephone company had, or might during the continuation of the agreement, establish telephone exchanges. That agreement was then in existence, under which the Bell Telephone Company had an exclusive right to the Canadian Pacific Railway stations, limiting it to these particular stations. When application was made to the Railway Commission, the Railway Commissioners, that is to say Mr. Blair, held that they were entitled to access. The only question in dispute was as to whether this exclusive contract was a valid contract, that is to say, the exclusive contract between the telephone company and the railway company ; and whether or not, it being an exclusive contract,

the compensation provided for by this section had to be considered from the standpoint of that exclusive contract-whether or not they were
obliged to pay compensation for damages that might result to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company as a result of the violation of that exclusive contract. Now, Mr. Blair held that that contract was not a contract in restraint of trade, that it was a good contract, and that if the municipalities of Port Arthur and Fort William desired to get access, in estimating the compensation, the damage resulting from the violation of that contract would have to be taken into account. The right of access was not denied, the only dispute was as to the question of compensation.
In the light of this clause.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In the light of that clause. Now it might be well to quote the words of the judgments of the commissioners. Mr. Blair held :
That the said agreement was valid and not void or voidable as being in restraint of trade or against public policy, and that an order made under section 193 should provide for payment of compensation upon just terms for all lawful rights and interests injuriously affected thereby.
Mr. Bernier held :
While the agreement is valid, and compensation should therefore he allowed, the question of compensation should be reserved for future .consideration, and determined after hearing any case that might be presented by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company or any other railway company in support of damages.
' After hearing any case.' Mr. Bernier and Mr. Blair decided the railway had a right of access. As to the right of access there is no dispute. But they both held that this exclusive contract is to be taken into account in estimating the damage. Mr. Mills held :
That the agreement is in restraint of trade and against public policy, and that compensation should be awarded only for the use of the premises occupied by the applicants' telephones and the expense of operating them.
So you see what the result of this judgment is, merely that two commissioners held this agreement good and an other held it had. and that the two commissioners who held the agreement good and as not being in restraint of trade, say that that agreement must be taken into account in estimating the damages. That is all that is decided in that case, and nothing more.
Then will the Minister of Justice say whether he will accept my amendment ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I cannot accept the amendment, I do not see why I should. I do not think my hon. friend's amendments, if accepted, would carry him very much further. If the object he has in view is, as I presume it is, to enable the telephone com-1 pany to obtain access to the railway station

in violation of an existing agreement and without compensation. I am opposed to such legislation as that. If there is a legal contract that is to be violated as a result of the enforcement of section 193 in regard to these rights, any damage that may result in violation of that contract must be admitted. If that is what he has in view I am opposed to it.
Cannot this House declare what is in restraint of trade ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think that would be rather a dangerous thing to .do, in view of the fact that our courts have been engaged for the past twently-five or thirty years in construing contracts made in restraint of trade.
Surely the telephone company did not want access without paying damages.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is what my hon. friend from East York wants.
But the telephone company itself would not want that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It wanted access on agreeing to pay compensation for locating their telephone system, but without regard to the violation of this contract.
I think there must be some misunderstanding.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Let the hon. gentleman read the judgments.
I am sure they would make an offer to pay damages.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.
Could not the commission have made an order allowing access upon the payment of damages ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The order has gone, the question of compensation being left open to be determined.
What is the telephone company complaining about ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I don't know.

I cannot agree with the argument that this agreement between the railway company and the telephone company is a good agreement, that it should be respected, that it should be considered, in view of this condition, which is a general condition-general at least in my part of the country-that the Bell Company has no telephone in the railway station, but that it has a right under that agreement to have a telephone there and to prevent anybody else from having a telephone there. The argument means that when a local telephone company wishes to connect with the Canadian Pacific Railway stations this local company would have to pay damages because of the violation of an agreement between the railway company and ti\e Bell Telephone Mr. FITZPATRICK.
Company, when the Bell Telephone Company had not done anything under that agreement and had suffered no injury whatever.
If there was no injury there would be no damage.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Exactly.
And if it were not installed I can see the damages would be merely nominal.

I maintain there should be no admission of any damages in such a case, and if the argument is that there are damages in such a case, then I for one say that the law should be amended, and that no such a thing should be permitted ; that where the public interest or the public use requires the entry of the telephone system which is established in that part of the country, into the railway station, no agreement between the telephone company and the railway company should be held good which would prevent that free access.
You would not want us to steal your property would you ? Neither must you ask us to steal other people's property.
Whose property is being stolen ?
By the Bell Telephone ?

Not at all, they have no property. If the argument is that the railway company's property is being stolen or being taken or used without their consent, I can understand it, but that is not the claim. The telephone company is prepared to pay for the use of the railway company's property, or for any inconvenience to which the railway company may be put. The question is as to the Bell Telephone Company's property, and I say that the telephone company has no property in such a case, even though they have an agreement, or if that agreement is good in. law, the law should be changed so that it shall not be good.

And the hon. Minister of Justice by a single amendment could introduce into this House a declaration that a railway company enfranchised! by this parliament, given all these powers and subsidies shall not discriminate against any of its patrons or the public in the use of its station^ for Bthe furtherance of the trade and commerce of this country. We could pass that law in two seconds here, we could reach that grievance, we could declare that these railway companies shall not do that, but instead of that we allow them to do anything they like, we allow them to entrench themselves behind these contracts and when an effort is made to get some kind of remedy for the people these contracts made by companies enfranchised by this parliament against the public interest are pleaded. We have

given enormous subsidies to these companies, we have given them land and money and for every one million dollars represented a third of it came out of the pockets of the people, not to mention the lands ; yet these companies have the effrontery to make this agreement and when the public ask under the law to have telephonic communication with the stations they say to them : You must do your business through the Bell Telephone Company, another monopoly allied with us in keeping our yoke upon the necks of the people. This is an infamous contract. It should never be allowed in any country and the people ask that it be rescinded. The Liberal party should rise up and declare that any contract that is against the public interest, is against the advancement of trade, is against the welfare of the people but instead of that it is pleaded : Contract, contract, go to the courts ; no remedy can be bad here. If we have any vestige of regard for the duty for which we have been sent here, let us approach this problem earnestly. We are not here to get through with our duties so that we may get away on our holidays ; we are here to try and cure this grievance and I appeal to the government, if they have no remedy to suggest. Will they not say to these creatures that we have created, to these railway companies :	You
must treat the people fairly ? if yon let one section of the community into your railway station y$u must let them all in. You must give the same privilege to all these telephone companies arid you must give an interchange of traffic with the Bell Telephone Company provided they pay you a. reasonable compensation. A year or two ago the bon Minister of Justice promised the people that he would bring down a general law dealing with all these telephone companies. The telephone is the greatest public convenience to-day. The people want to use it. We want to extend its use to every one, to increase the comfort of all by extending this line to levery man, to every farmer ; but, while this should be our desire, the use of tbe telephone is almost prohibited by reason of the infamous and unfair agreement which is at present existing between these great railway corporations and the Bell Telephone Company. The Grand Trunk Railway to which we have given a credit to the value of $150,000,000 are parties to this agreement. If we had had any of the instinct in us of the men who have fought the people's battles in former days we would have said to this Grand Trunk Railway Company : Not one dollar of public money shall be given you; not one piece of legislation shall we give to you until you cancel that infamous agreement. Sir Thos. Sbaughnessy, president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, has practically confessed in public that if he were forced to do it he would withdraw this agreement. If the right hon. Prime Minister would sit down in his private cabinet and say :	My dear Shaughnessy, the contract which exists between you and the Bell Telephone Company is against the public interest, it is a tyranny, it is a matter of slavery as far as the people are concerned and if you do not cancel it we will have to introduce legislation declaring it to be against the public interest. The remedy would be found. But, nothing of that kind is being done. No remedy is granted. It is the old story of pleading contracts, pleading vested rights, and telling the people to go to the courts. They have created this court at an enormous expense, they have provided situations for all these men, the farmers and the people generally are taxed to pay the salaries of these men and I would call 'the attention of my hon. friend the Postmaster General to the fact -I do not want him to turn away from me now-that the people are paying these taxes are providing these salaries, are granting these subsidies, are giving these railway companies franchises, are giving them lands, are giving thetn money and are giving them further powers to borrow money, making them greater and stronger than they are today, allowing them to pay immense dividends as the Bell Telephone Company is, while we have not the courage to tell these corporations that they must treat the people fairly, and that they must deal out equal justice to all. What does my hon. friend from South Brant (Mr. Heyd) say about it ? The people of Brantford have decided on a municipal telephone system of their own. (Brantford is a great city. It is one of the finest cities in Canada, a city the export trade of which is next to and almost exceeds the export trade of the city of Toronto. It is a city composed of enterprising men, factories are built, fine houses are being erected, great business houses are being put up and all that the men of Brantford say is ? Let us have access to the railway station for our municipal telephone system. The answer to that is : You cannot put your municipal telephone system into the Grand Trunk office ; you cannot put it into the Canadian Pacific Railway office. It is a regrettable fact that tbe late Minister of Railways and Canals, having given his solemn pledge to this House that the clause now under discussion would practically meet the grievance that I have raised, when he came to interpret it as the judge in the case, should place upon it an interpretation differing from that which he led me and others to think would be the result of the amendment. But, I appeal to hon. gentlemen opposite. I appeal to this House. I do not want to make an issue of politics out of it, but I do appeal to this House to sit down and see if we cannot find a remedy for this grievance by which we can compel these companies not to do anything wrong, not to lose any money, but to treat the people fairly and to give them justice. These companies are our creatures.

k
They are not greater than parliament, and above all things they are just as much committed to treat the public justly as any one else. We want justice for all-fair treatment, no discrimination. We want this section so changed as to permit access to the railway station by every section of the community. If one telephone company can get in. all telephone companies should be permitted to get in. We have passed a law pi'o-viding that every railway company shall grant equal express facilities to all companies. Why is this provision not extended to telephone companies? I leave my case there. ,1 put it before the House. Personally, it is a very small consideration to me, but it is a very great consideration to the hon. Postmaster General who proposes shortly to appeal to the voters of Markham whom I have the honour to represent and it does mean something to my hon. friend from Brantford.
You asked me what I say. I say that the agreement between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Bell Telephone Company is in restraint of trade.

Hear, hear. I am very glad to hear the hon. gentleman say that and probably some good is coming out of this discussion. I believe it is in restraint of trade and I believe it is the duty of the House forthwith to declare that the agreement is in the restraint of trade. It is not our duty to send it to the courts. Why send everything to the courts ? What is this parliament for ? Is a parliament not for the remedy of grievances ? I have said in this House before and I say it again, that the whole history of British constitutional progress is made up of the rectification of all kinds of grievances by parliament, not through courts so much as by the acts of parliament, a .change in the law, a violation of contracts that may have been entered into and an interference with vested rights. The men who had the monopolies in the time of Queen Bess all claimed that they had these monopolies under their franchises but the public interest was declared to override these rights and one after the other the monopolies were removed. This was the course of British constitutional progress. But we in this parliament say now that there must be an end in the way of legislation ; it must be a question for the courts to interpret, and any such thing as special relief must not be afforded. Let us stop that. We have the facts, these towns have the grievances. It is the old case of the citizens, the burgesses, coming to parliament for relief, asking in this case simply that their own municipal system, which they bought with their own money, shall be allowed to have access to the Canadian Pacific Railway station. Is the Grand Trunk Railway, which we are creating, to turn against the people of Canada too ? Is Mr. Mr. MACLEAN.
Hays's new Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, the Canadian National Transportation system which is to be built with $150,000,000 of the credit of the people of this country to close its stations to any kind of access to municipal telephone systems ? What would happen to-morrow if the Postmaster General decided to nationalize the telegraph and telephone systems of this country ? Would he for one moment allow that contract of the Grand Trunk Railway and Canadian Pacific Railway to stand ?
He could not help himself.

Yes he could help himself, he could declare that contract at an end, taking the line that it was against the public interest and he would force these roads to let him into their stations. They could not bar him out, and the whole people of Canada would support him. I say it is a matter of negotiation. We have these companies at our mercy. The Bell Telephone Company are here every day seeking legislation and we could say to them : You must abandon this iniquitous contract and must treat every one fairly, equitably and without discrimination. There are a dozen ways of getting at that; what is wanted is the determination to do it, to rectify the grievance. I leave my case as I have tried to present it. Perhaps I have presented it with some heat but I have tried to present it in the interests of the public and without doing any injustice to these companies. I do not propose to do any injustice to them. They are making money and they can afford to treat the people that created them, fairly, equitably and without discriminating against one in favour of the other. No harm is done by making them play fair.
Fair play is bonnie play.
You can do it by legislation or in a dozen other ways, but in some way immediate relief ought to be granted.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I quite agree with my hon. friend who has just taken his seat that fair play is bonnie play, but fair play means fair play to all parties.
Hear, hear.	,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not that the strong man should take the weaker man by the throat. But let us see now what my hon. friend wants. What he calls fair play is for parliament to authorize a railway company, the Canadian Pacific Railway-to deal with the specific case under discussion-to violate its contract and to violate it with impunity, in spite of the fact that that contract has been declared by this court, the Board of Railway Commissioners, a valid and legal contract. He wants us to do that and calls it fair play.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no fair play in giving authority, to one party to a contract to violate it. That is not legislation which this House would sanction; no body of men would sanction such legislation. My suggestion is this : It is important first of all to see to it that all telephone companies in this country have equal facilities on equal terms with respect to access to all railway stations. That is important undoubtedly. Now the Canadian Pacific Railway have an exclusive contract with the Bell Telephone Company by virtue of which the Bell Telephone Company have arrangements with this company which practically gives them a monopoly, and as a result other telephone companies are excluded from the Canadian Pacific Railway stations. If the judgment of the Railway Commission is a good judgment, that is the present condition of affairs. As I said before when this question was up that judgment, as I understood, was being appealed from to the Supreme Court. Some doubts have been expressed on that point and having made inquiries I find that it is not at all certain that steps have been taken to that end.' I would advise, subject of course to conference with my colleagues, that the question should first be settled, whether or not, under the existing agreement of the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Grand Trunk Railway with the Bell Telephone Company, that company have an exclusive right to the use of these railway stations. They have not that exclusive right if that exclusive contract is not a good contract, and if it is so declared by the Supreme Court the matter ends, because the legislation we now have is quite sufficient to give all the facilities required to any telephone company. If, on the contrary, the Supreme Court decides that the contract is a good contract, that a violation of that contract would mean that one of the parties to it would be placed in the invidious position of having the right by statute to violate its contract, I say that we should take pains to carefully take what steps are necessary. I admit that that would be serious, but not so serious or intricate that this parliament could not deal with it. We could find a remedy for such a condition, but let us find out first where we stand. Let us find out if it be true that this Bell Company have an exclusive monopoly of access to these stations. If the municipality has not taken an appeal from the judgment of the Board of Railway Commissioners let the government undertake to do it, and have the question settled once and for all. After all there is not very much out of the way in this course because this is the only contract of the sort in existence in this country, and it is of importance, I admit, that at this present time equal facilities should be given to all telephone companies, to all express companies, in fact to the whole general public in the use of our great means of transportation. All of our
railway facilities must be put at the disposal of tfll persons and corporations on the same terms. That is a correct principle and to that extent I go with my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean). There is no necessity in the assertion of a correct principle to do an injustice, and it would be doing an injustice to give one party to a contract, a statutory right to violate that contract to the detriment of the other party and to such legislation as that I cannot give my consent.
It has been done : bad contracts have been declared bad contracts.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Let this contract be declared a bad contract, but not by parliament. My hon. friend will not get any thinking man in this House to sanction any undertaking to substitute parliament for the courts in the construction of contracts.
But this parliament will declare that it is a wrong contract.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is a vicious principle.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think that the Minister of Justice has not quite given my hon. friend from York (Mr. Maclean) credit for the way in which he approaches this subject. I do not think that my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) desires to interfere with the sanctity of contracts. I do not understand his position to be exactly that. I understand his position to be neither this, that these two companies, which may be said to exercise to a certain ^xtent monopolies, with regard to transportation of passengers and freight on the one hand, and with regard to the transmission of intelligence on the other hand, should not be allowed to make a contract between themselves so as to impose an undue restriction, virtually a tax, upon access to the station of the railway company. That is a position which commends itself to some of us in the House. We must respect the sanctity of contracts ; but with regard to these virtual monopolies, we interfere so far with their unrestricted rights to make contracts that we do not allow a railway company to charge more than a certain amount, and, so far as telephone companies are concerned, we require their tariffs of tolls to be approved by the Governor in Council. While we must respect the sanctity of contracts, we at the same time say that no arrangement ought to be made between two corporations possessing these monopolies by which the people through independent companies are restricted from that means of communication with the railway stations throughout the country which is so desirable in the public interest. For my part, I am very sorry that the towns of Port Arthur and Fort William did not go on and have the
<5743

Railway Commission determine what compensation is really payable. It strikes me that if I were sitting on that commission, I should not fix the amount of compensation at any very large figure. I have looked over the report which the Minister of Justice has been good enough to hand me, and I find the following claims put in by the counsel of one of the companies :
The results to the benefit of Canadian Pacific Railway :
Passes and franks over Bell Company's long distance lines, valued
at	$18,297 00
Exchange service, 774 instruments free to railway company, valued at	 22,652 00

On the other side of the account we have:
To the benefit of the Bell Company :
Trips, annual and periodical passes over Canadian Pacific Railway,
valued at	$22,258 00
Refunds	?	 200 00

It seems to be on such a statement as this that the idea of large compensation was based before the commission. I do not myself see how access by the two municipal corporations to that railway station would interfere very much with the condition of things that prevailed between these two companies, and I would be inclined to think that if the railway commission came to fix the amount of damages, it would have to be merely nominal. I agree Avith the idea put forward by my hon. friend from Toronto and with what has Jjeen said by my hon. friend the Minister of Justice as well. I agree absolutely that we must abide by the sanctity of contracts; but when we come to deal with great corporations exercising what are virtually monopolies, we must at the same time ip the public interest restrain these corporations from making contracts which are not in the public interest. On the one hand, they get very great privileges from parliament, and on the other hand, they must be content to have those privileges so controlled as to give the public its full rights in every respect.

f.ystem cannot have access to the railway stations, it is practically useless. When the Question was up before, I drew attention to these facts. Since then the Bell Telephone Company have strung a wire from Cardston to Edmonton along that 300 miles of railway, and I presume are in a position of entrenched monopoly in every railway station. If those fourteen towns now existing and fourteen more rapidly growing wish to have a local telephone system, they will find themselves in this difficulty, that they will be debarred from access to the railway stations. The question thus comes closely home to the people. We are simply in the hands of the Bell Telephone Company, and that company has the monopoly in the district of Alberta from end to end. There is no doubt that the people there could estab lish a local service which would give very much cheaper rates than can any company which looks to a profit; and to prevent their getting access to the railway stations is to prevent their spending their own money In providing their own telephone accommodation. It is evident, therefore, that the agreement between the Bell Telephone and the railway companies is a trespass on the rights of the people, and ibis parliament will be doing less than its duty if it does not take measures to relieve the people from that injustice.
As regards precedents, let me call attention to the fact that not many years ago the whole grain trade of the Northwest was in the hands of a ring of elevator owners because of an agreement between them and the Canadian Pacific Railway. The Canadian Pacific Railway refused to handle any grain except through these elevators. They refused to give sites at railway stations except to elevators of a certain capacity, and the result was that the people were robbed of hundreds of thousands of dollars every year. When that question was brought up in this House I remember that those of us who demanded the free right of shipping grain were denounced as socialists ; but to-day there is a law on the statute-book which enables every farmer to obtain shipping of his grain at any railway station in his turn.
And that was brought about by an Act of parliament, and not by a decision of the courts.

There was no decision of the courts annulling the agreement between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the elevators. There was no change in the conditions, but parliament, in its wisdom, decided that that agreement was a trespass on the rights of the people and annulled it.

I desire to say a word or two, as I did not have the opportunity of fully explaining my position. I have said that in my opinion the agreement between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Bell Telephone Company is an agreement: in restraint of trade. I am quite willing to take my
law from the Minister of Justice ; but whet', it comes to determining what is right as between man and man, I propose to exercise my own intelligence. The Canadian Pacific Railway and the Bell Telephone Company have the legal power to make the agreement they have entered into, and there is nothing to prevent the Bell Telephone Company making just such an agreement with every other railway in the country. But if that is legally right, it is morally wrong ; and if anything else of the kind be attempted, I shall vote against it; and if any proposition be made to declare that this agreement, no matter what the law may be, is in restraint of trade and injurious to the general public, I shall certainly support it.

If the contention put forth by some lion, members be correct, then there is, no use of parliament meeting at all. If these contracts entered into by different corporations are sacred and cannot be touched, no matter how much they may conflict with the interests of the people, then there is no use in parliament sitting and we had better disband at once. But I contend that parliament is not helpless in this matter. When the people are suffering from an injustice, parliament has a perfect right to apply the remedy. Here is a grievance brought before us by the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean). It is a grievance of which we all have knowledge. Yet we are told that the courts are the only one to decide, and that parliament is helpless. If that be the case, what is the use of bringing the representatives of the people together every year ?

I want to put myself right. I sympathize thoroughly with my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean i in his zeal, and likewise with the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Robinson) and the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Heyd). If there is a wrong, we must endeavour to correct it, and correct it in the proper way. It would be very strange indeed if in the attempt to remedy one wrong we should commit another and a greater one. The hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) need not think that this discussion has not been useful. It has been of value, because it has brought before the members the facts
I did not say the discussion was of no use.

My hon. friend seemed to think that because we all did not agree on a solution of the difficulty therefore our discussion was of no value. But I think that although we do not all agree on the remedy proposed by the hon. member for East York, it is well that the facts should be brought before us, because in my opinion there is sufficient ability in the House to arrive at a conclusion within the four corners of the law which will do justice to everybody. The Minister of Justice, I think, appealed to the sound sense of every

man when he said that parliament should not be asked to violate contracts. I agree with the hon. minister in this : Parliament, Sir, should he the preserver of contracts. We must set an example to the whole of Canada by preserving contracts and doing the right. The hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) said that he was willing to compensate the Canadian Pacific Railway. But, the trouble is, that the Canadian Pacific Railway have assigned their rights to the Bell Telephone Company, as I understand the matter, and so, compensation must be made to the Bell Company. I will meet the difficulties as I come to them but I am free to say this that it would be an awful thing if we had no control over these corporations. We have control over them, and we will master them, every one of them ; but we must do it according to the principles of right and justice.
How ?

The thing is as clear as daylight. But we must go at it intelligently. To ask parliament to strike down contracts is revolutionary. We ought not to be permitted to sit for twenty-four hours, if we do that. Recollect, the Bell Telephone Company have acquired property from the Canadian Pacific Railway, and for that property they have given value. Are we to steal that property ? Why, I would as soon break into a bank to-night, as agree to a proposition of that kind. If I were to agree to such a proposition, I would be a public thief-neither more or less. But there is a way to do it and that way has been pointed out. I admire the zeal of my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean).
But you say I am a pirate.
No, I will restrain my hon. friend from being a pirate. He is too good a man to be a pirate.
Tell us how to control the corporations.	.

I will. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) has pointed out the way. It is perfectly simple. The court has decided that this is a legal contract. My hon. friend from South Brant (Mr. Heyd) says it is not. Well, let them appeal the decision. If the court decides that this is a contract in restraint of trade, then, it will be void and the whole thing will be settled at once. But, if the courts say that this is a valid and legal contract, would you propose to steal the property of the Bell Telephone Company ? For, that is what you would be doing, just as much as if I were to ask parliament to take away my hon. friend's (Mr. Maclean's) property in ' The World ' newspaper and give it to me, and parliament were to do so.

May I ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Gourley) one question ? If a Mr. GOURLEY.
man were to steal a horse and sell it to another, would' the sanctity of contract allow the purchaser to hold the property ?
That will not do ; give me a parallel case.
It is a parallel case to this. The Canadian Pacific Railway have stolen the rights of others and sold them to the Bell Telephone Company.

If that is so, the Supreme Court of Canada will decide, at once, that this contract is against public policy, and, therefore, void. If the hon. gentleman is right in his facts the court is the place for him.

Before dinner I was endeavouring to show why we ought not to adopt the remedy that is proposed here, and ns I was closing some of my friends on this side asked me. Well, what is the remedy ? I think it is very simple. Here is a judgment, declaring that the Bell Telephone Company have a vested interest in this contract. Then how do you deal with vested interests ? The case is not different from that of a man owning land by title deed ; be is not in a better position than if he owned property under contract. Supposing this judgment stands, you must face the position that this company holds property under a contract. If you want the property and must pay compensation, and the compensation is too heavy for the private corporations, of the towns of Port Arthur and T ort William to bear, then you come to parliament and say :	Here is a case arising
under a contract under which the damages have become so heavy that it is improper to ask a private corporation to bear them. Declare tnat these contracts are void, but declare them void in the same manner as you would if you wanted land of any other property for the public use ; say that while you rescind that contract it must be done upon compensation, the same as if you were taking any other man's property. That is one way. If you do not appeal from this judgment you must take that position. But I think the member for Halifax hit the mark pretty well when he said : Why did not these gentlemen have the damages assessed ? It is true that the telephone company put in an extravagant bill before the commission for damages. But you know how these things are trumped up. If these damages had to be assessed, the commission might have introduced a measure of damages that would in the end make the amount very small, they might have given the telephone company very small damages for an abridgment of their rights under that eon-

tract. Therefore I think what the company should have done, what the town should have done, would have been to go before the Railway Commission and have the damages assessed. Then the company would have been in a very good position, and small damages would have been paid them. But if the damages were large and onerous, or if it were likely that this same principle or measure of damagp would extend to all the towns in the commnu.ty, then you would (have an excellent ground upon which to come to parliament and say : Owing to the legislation of this parliament, owing to the fact that you have created companies in this country and given them rights which interfere with tlie public weal, therefore this parliament must deal with them, and this parliament must rescind those contracts, but do it by giving them compensation.
That would be one position to take, and my bon. friend would be right in taking it. But I am sorry to differ with him, because he is so anxious for the public welfare, and on this occasion he made a strong appeal to my sympathy and I would be glad to support him in almost any 'scheme. But I could not support him in a scheme that would lead to a breach of all that was right and proper. Now then if you appealed, I think that would be a proper course to pursue. Some hon. gentlemen have alleged that it would be too onerous to compel these towns to carry on heavy lawsuits. That will be a good ground for asking the Minister of Justice in a case of this jkind to assume the work of settlement, and have the appeal borne by the Crown. I think the Minister of Justice would accede to that if he thought it would be too onerous, for these towns to carry on these appeals. Let the minister appeal and have the principle settled whether that contract is sound, whether it confers rights or whether. as one hon. member has snid, it is against public policy and should be forfeited. If it is settled that the contract is void, then all our difficulties are over. If on the other hand it is settled that the contract confers rights of property, we would have to deal with it again, and these people would have to come to parliament. If the appeal is taken, they should first go before the commission in order to get the damages settled so that both the question of damages and the principle should be settled on the appeal. Then if the damages were held to be of a serious character, and I understand this difficulty extends over the whole country, that would be an excellent ground on which to come to parliament and say : Asa result of your legislation private rights are being sacrificed, and no private individual should be called upon to suffer loss, therefore, come to our aid with a Bill of indemnity. But if. as I have said, the case were appealed and the expense borne by the Crown, we would know what the meas-215	[DOT]
ure of damages were and whether the contract was a good one. If the contract was void, there would be an end of the matter. If the damages were trifling, the town could pay them. If the court sustained a measure of damages that was likely to lead to serious consequences that would be a ground upon which gentlemen could come to parliament and say :	Owing to the legislation
of this parliament, private corporations have thrown upon towns in this country, a burden too onerous for them to bear. In that ease I would gladly vote with my hon friend to take such a course as the wisdom of parliament would seem just to the town as well as to Hie corporations.

We hear a good deal in this House about vested rights and very little about vested wrongs. It does not matter what wrong is perpetrated on the public by a corporation. As soon as they acquire a foothold then vested rights begin. Now if a man goes and squats on your property, what will you do ? You will eject him at the earliest opportunity. If a corporation does the same thing, and acquires or becomes improperly vested in what belongs to you, have you not a right to resort to the same remedy ? Is there any justifiable reason why you should pay money for a right that has been improperly acquired ? You might as well tell me that if a man steals your horse and goes and sells it to another man, you have no right to go and demand it back. It would be as reasonable to say that you must pay for that horse as to say that the Bell Telephone Company must be paid for the rights which they improperly secured and which, according to the policy and intention of parliament, it was never intended they should have. The clear policy and intention of parliament has always been, so far as I have understood, that a corporation such as a railway corporation, must give equal rights and equal facilities to all doing business with that corporation. We give it a franchise, we give it great power, we give it a subsidy and many other valuable considerations for the purpose of enabling it to serve the public. But it must serve them all alike, and each one is entitled to the same consideration in doing their business with that corporation. These railway companies become common carriers, and every member of the community who does any business with them has a right to equal treatment. All who travel over their railway or who send freight over it, have a right to be dealt with in the same manner. We have over and over again provided by law, and by amendments to laws, that there shall be no discrimination in favour of one as against another, in favour of one locality as against another locality. That principle is so well understood in parliament that it is almost waste of time to talk about it. It has been adopted over and over again by



both parties. To-day, we are dealing with a railway company that is not giving every individual in the community tlie same chances to do their business over that line. That railway corporation we create, and according to our policy, and according to the intention of parliament, that railway corporation is required to deal equitably with all and extend the same rights and the same privileges to all.
They have sold rights belonging to one portion of the community to another portion of the community for consideration. Then you ask those who have been precluded from the enjoyment of these rights to buy out the individual to whom the railway company have improperly sold them. These are the vested rights which they claim and these are the damages which the railway company must be paid. To whom ? Not to the railway company for the privilege of putting the telephone line into their station but to the Bell Telephone Company which have improperly become possessed of rights that belong to every other member of the community. Suppose there were one hundred people living along the line of the Bell Telephone Company. Every one of these individuals enjoys the advantage of being able to communicate with the railway station for the purpose of doing business, inquiring about the trains, inquiring about trade and inquiring about many other things, but there are hundreds who have not the advantage of being on that line. The other line upon which they are located runs right to the railway station, but they are deprived of putting the -telephone into the station because this other corporation have been sold the sole right to do it. Those who' use the new line are deprived of the privilege that parliament intended they should enjoy, they are deliberately discriminated against and then to add insult to injury they are asked before they shall be allowed to put their telephone into the station to pay damages ? To whom? Not to the railway company who might be expected to grant some consideration but to the other corporation who have taken away the rights that properly belongs to them. Is that fair or reasonable ? Was that what this parliament gave that charter to this and other railway companies for ? Was that what parliament intended when it gave the right to the Bell Telephone Company to plant lines all over the country ? It was not. Parliament reserved to itself the right to control their rates for fear that they might be unreasonable. They have a limit up to which they may go, but they cannot go beyond that. So it is with the railway company. We control both of them, but now we are asked, when they have stolen rights belonging to the community, to turn around and pay for the goods which have been stolen from us. Is parliament prepared to sanction or support that ? I do not think so. As I said before if our Mr. SPROULE.
efforts were as much directed towards the redress of vested wrongs as they are towards the protection of what are called vested rights, but which are in reality vested wrongs we would be more appropriately doing our duty to the great mass of people. The Bell Telephone Company have become a very great monopoly to-day and a very onerous one. They have been acting of late years as if there were no authority in the land to control them and almost-I- was going to say-in an insolent way as if they felt that they were masters of the situation. They are strengthening themselves in every direction, and if they continue in the future for a reasonable length of time at the same rate that they have been progressing in the past in the direction of infringing upon the rights of the people, they will soon be an uncontrollable monopoly which will respect no person's rights or interests in the country. To give an idea of what they are aiming at, I wish to draw the attention of the committee for a short time to an item which appears in to-day's papers. I have the Toronto 1 World ' before me, and it contains the following :-
Independent Companies warned they must sell out or he driven to the wall.
The threat is thrown out.
Chicago, July 13.-A gigantic $20,000,000 telephone trust is being organized by the Bell Telephone Company to control lines in the states of Illinois, Indiana, Michigan and Ohio.
And I presume elsewhere because they are not going to stop at these states.
Independent telephone companies operating within the district will be bought up or driven to the wall.
They have their opinion as to which alternative to accept.
The Indiana Independent Telephone Company at Laporte, representing the telephone systems in operation in Indiana and Michigan, received a private report to-day apprising the officers of the plans for the formation of the trust and warning them that the blow is directed against that and all other companies.
It is said on good authority that the sum of $20,000,000 has been placed at the disposal of the men Interested in forming the trust and that more can be secured by them if necessary.
The Bell Telephone Company, it is alleged, is determined to drive out of existence in one way or another every competing company in the states that interferes with its monopoly.
What they are doing in the United States to-day, they are doing in Canada as well. Their plans are being laid. They are operating along the same lines; they are throwing out their lines in every direction. They are becoming possessed of one right ber.e and another right there, and the greater

tlie value of tlie rights which they become possessed of the more difficult it will be to dislodge them in the future. Will parliament now be equal to the occasion when the rights of the citizens are invaded by this gigantic monopoly and stop them when they are on the threshold of their operations ? This is the time to do it. If we do not do it now it will be found that delays are dangerous. We are told to take this matter to this court or to that court, to take to the Supreme. Court and if the Supreme Court does not decide according to our wish, to to take it to the Privy Council. That is just what they want. Delay from month to month suits their purpose. If it passed over for another year they have secured the advantages to be gained in that time. They are strengthening their hands in the meantime, they are making more difficult the task that we have to perform at some time. My hon. friend from Colchester (Mr. Gour-lcy) said :	They should be compensated.
We want the damages assessed. What damages ? Damages for that which they stole from the people, damages for stolen rights ? That is what they want. These rights belong to all of the people. The Canadian Pacific Railway have no right to dispose of the privileges which parliament said all the people should enjoy, not a portion of the people but the whole people, not the parties enjoying the advantages of the Bell Telephone Company's service, but every one who utilizes the services of the railway company. Then, we shall assess the damages in the interest of whom ? In the interest of the parties who are in possession of the stolen property to-day ? We must pay them for that which they have got froffi us. It is a strange principle to advocate. It is not a view that will commend itself to the common sense of the people of this country. I say that we have no reason to respect these rights. This measure is not a confiscation, it does not interfere or take away any private vested right because there are no vested rights that they should, enjoy or be paid for. It is said that if you take away a man's land in the work of building a railway you have to pay him for it. Yes, but that man got his land honestly when he bought it from the Crown or from some one else. He bought it in a proper and legitimate way, he gave value for it and he has the right that the state concedes to him m any part of the country. But this is a corporation right of an entirely different character. This corporation have become possessed of rights that belong to other members of the community and that parliament has declared to belong to other members of the community. Yet we are asked to buy them back. Why should we buy them back? I say the country cannot understand that. As long as we tamper with it, as long as we allow this corporation to feloniously take possession of our rights, so long will we be held as slaves in the matter. There is a growing feeling against cor-2153
porations in this country because of their infringements upon the rights of individuals and of the impossibility of getting any redress. It is said that there are the courts in the country, but the individual is too weak to fight them. It is impossible for him to carry this fight from court to court. He cannot employ lawyers that charge large fees and he has to suffer under the wrong inflicted upon him if the state will not come to his assistance.
The state has the right to come to his assistance. It is for that purpose that parliament is convened ; that is one of the duties of parliament and if parliament fails to do its duty then the great tribunal of the country must be appealed and the education of the people will go on until such a sentiment is reached in the country that no parliament can withstand it, or if they attempt to go they will be driven out so quickly that they will not know what has happened to them. I hold that when the Act was passed we did an improper thing in inserting that clause which gave that colourable right which *they enjoy to-day and which prevented that commission from taking away that right. Now we are told that under that clause of the Act we have not the right to interfere. The country thought that we were to enjoy that right under that Act. Parliament said that we were to enjoy that right yet we find now by the interpretation of lawyers and of the courts that we do not enjoy it. Then I say it is our duty to amend the Act so as to give to the people of the country the enjoyment of that right which parliament intended they should enjoy and this I submit ought to be the policy of both parties in this House at all times.

During recess, I went to the library to see if I could find an authority in regard to the jurisdiction of parliament in this matter. I found this most excellent authority which I shall x'ead to the House :
The principles of parliamentary government are such that we are bound to believe that the people through their representatives will deal with every grievance ; and the attempt to get behind the people's representatives, to create some other tribunal, to take the place of parliament, especially in matters of money, and to give that body power independent of the government and parliament, to deal with these matters, is a step in the wrong direction ; and we on this side of the House are not prepared to take it.
That is excellent doctrine ; that doctrine was declared in this House yesterday and it is the doctrine of the Minister of Finance. Yesterday this House was told that parliament was the instrument to remedy the grievances of the people, that we did not want these grievances sent to Exchequer courts but that they were to be settled in this House. Only yesterday was that doctrine laid down here ; it is good doctrine and I adhere to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Did you vote for it .yesterday ?

And so on. There is the agreement and le substance of it is that the Bell Te e-hone Company give certain services to the tilway company in return for certain n'vices Now if we declare, as we ou0ht ^ declare, that that contract is against ublic interest, no harm will be done. We

will be interfering only with two companies which we have created. We will be doing nothing prejudicial to the public; we simply say to these two creatures of parliament: In the exercise of the powers which we gave you, you have done something contrary to the public interest and we declare that what you have done in that connection is illegal and is null and void. No damage is done to the companies ; instead of exchanging services they give money to one another. The cheques cancel one another and no injustice is done. That is a reasonable proposition. But instead of that, we have all this lecturing about sacred rights and the sanctity of contracts, and men who stand up for the public rights are charged with being pirates and robbers. When hon. gentlemen talk about the sanctity of contracts,
I ask them, what about the sanctity of public rights, which is above the sanctity of contracts any day. There is another way out of the difficulty, and that is by negotiation. These two railway companies and this telephone company are suppliants for legislation of some kind or another at every session of this parliament. The Grand Trunk is a petitioner here to-day ; the Canadian Pacific Railway is here every session as a suitor, and so is the Bell Telephone Company. They are all getting something, and the government can do with them what it . did in the case of the Crow's Nest Pass Railway. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company came and asked for a franchise and a subsidy, and the government said to them : When we give you these, you must abandon a certain right in regard to your rates which you claim to have to-day ; we will give you the franchise and the subsidy on that condition. And the Canadian Pacific Railway Company did it at once. The government is in a position to say to the Cf^nadian Pacific Railway, and the Bell Telephone Company: You must abandon that contract ; and there is a saving clause in it by which they can effect a settlement and remedy the grievance. As the Minister of Finance said last night : Parliament is the place to remedy the grievances of the people, and not the Exchequer Court or any other court. What is happening in Toronto to-day ? There is a company there with a charter which the Attorney General considers'is doing something against the public interest, and he is moving to cancel that charter. The company is pleading vested rights, and a judge of the High Court of Ontario gave judgment yesterday that the Crown as represented by the Attorney General had a perfect right to cancel a charter which it had given to a company because that company was doing something against the public interest. And the Crown, as represented by the Minister of Justice, could send for Sir Thomas Shaughnessy of the Canadian Pacific Railway and Senator McKay of the Bell Telephone Company, and say to them : Gentlemen, you are doing
something against the public interest, and if you do not rescind those contracts, I shall have to cancel your charter ; and he would be well within his right if he did so. If we only cancelled one of these charters in this country, you would see a much more humble attitude assumed by the companies than they assume to-day. They would realize that the people are more their masters than they thought they were. Now, I am through with the discussion, and what is to be done must be left to the judgment of the committee. I must tell my hon. friends that later on, when we come to the third reading,
I shall have to divide the House on the issue.

I do not think we are advancing our cause by abusing the Bell Telephone Company, accusing them of exercising stolen rights, and all that. We ought to look at this question from a business standpoint. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the Bell Telephone Company have both been chartered by this parliament, and I think parliament is able to control them. If they do what is wrong, or exceed their powers, this parliament will be able to take care of itself, and will see that that is done. As for the fear that they are going to spread out and control all the other telephone companies throughout the country,
I do not think there is any danger of that. This question has arisen quite recently, and I think there is a good deal in the contention of the hon. member for East York that there is a grievance. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the Bell Telephone Company have entered into an arrangement that is mutually satisfactory to themselves. They both concede rights to each other. The arangement has also been of great advantage to the public by enabling them to have the use of telephones in the railway stations all over the land. The Bell Telephone Company has done a great deal of good for the people of this country. If it were wiped out of existence to-morrow, we would find ourselves in a very bad mess indeed. But within the last year or two new conditions have arisen. New companies have started up. controlled largely by municipalities and private citizens, who have invested their money in them, and they desire access to the railway stations. Under these circumstances, it" is for us to consider what is best to be done. In my opinion, so far as the agreement between the Bell Telephone Company and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is concerned, it is nothing to us, so long as it does not interfere with the rights and privileges of the people. But the interests of the great public must be paramount over all others ; and this parliament is here, above everything else, to protect and guard and defend the rights of the people as a whole. These new companies are branching out in all directions ; they are becoming quite numerous. They are serv-I ing people who have not been served by the

other telephone companies, and it is in the interest of the public that they should have access to the stations not only of the Grand Trunk but of the Canadian Pacific Railway. This agreement stands in the way. Under the arrangement made between the two companies, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company cannot give these new companies access to its stations. Now, let us look at the facts. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company have made this agreement, which I think runs for six or seven years yet. Suppose it is renewed at the end of that time for eight or ten years longer. The vested rights of these companies continue ; and so it goes on, and the people are prevented from exercising their privileges and from getting the benefits they ought to have. I think therefore that the time has come when we should declare that, this agreement is not in the public interest. The hon member for Colchester (Mr. Gourley) suggested as a remedy that we should appeal this case to the Supreme Court for a decision. That would perhaps be the best course to pursue just now ; but I do not see that that is going to end the difficulty. Suppose the Supreme Court upheld the decision of the Railway Commission. If so, we would be just where we are to-day, and legislation would have to take effect after that. It seems to me that we might as well face the difficulty now as to wait for one or two or three years longer. There is no question but that the public will demand that this parliament grant these concessions which the public interest requires ; and it seems to me that instead of referring this matter to the Supreme Court the government should take immediate action and amend the law so as to enable all telephone companies to have the right of access to railway stations.

If I understood well what has been said this afternoon on both sides, the whole discussion may be summed up in a few words. We all admit that if this contract is legal, the Act must be amended. As my hon. friend from East York [Mr. Maclean) says, the contract is legal or it is not. But my hon. friend asks this House to decide that it is legal and take immediate action. Why, he asks, should we wait the decision of the Supreme Court ? Why not amend the Act at once ? That is a very practical way of putting the question. It is the way employed by the Yankees when they hang a man without giving him the benefit of a trial. But the Minister of Justice says that the proper means to take to decide whether the contract is legal or not is to refer the question to the Supreme Court. And he asks us to wait the decision of the Supreme Court before acting. That seems to be perfectly reasonable. Should the Supreme Court decide that the contract is not legal, then there will be no need to amend the law, because the law is suflicient

as it is. Should that court decide that the contract is legal, then we can proceed to amend the Act. And, as I have always stood by the law, as I have always had that respect for the law which every good citizen, and particularly every member of the legal profession, should have, I propose to stand by it now, and wait for the decision of the Supreme Court. Therefore, I shall vote against the amendment.

I cannot at all agree with the position taken by so many legal men of this House, that the case as between parliament and these companies is the same as it would be if between a private individual and these companies. Parliament, I submit, occupies an entirely different position. If there is a dispute between a private individual and these companies, if the towns of Port Arthur and Fort William have'a grievance against the Bell Telephone and the Canadian Pacific Railway companies, they must go to the courts. They did go to the Railway Commission and got judgment, from which judgment I presume the>
are entitled to appeal. But that has nothing whatever to do with our action, nor should it govern our action in any degree. We are responsible for the law under which that decision was rendered and under which the decision in appeal will be rendered. And if that law, for which we are responsible, does not give justice, the time and place to deal with the question is here and now. Plenty of evidence has been placed before [his parliament to-day to show that injustice has been and is being done and may be continued interminably. As to the charge that all those who desire to see justice done the public are law-breakers, or wish in any way to contravene the law, or infringe in any degree on the rights of any one, that charge is utterly unfounded. I am not a lawyer, but I will venture to state a first principle of law which will not be denied by any legal gentleman in this House, and which entirely covers this case. It is this, that a contract between any two parties entered into against the interests of a third party cannot be binding on that third party.
I would like any of the legal gentlemen to say whether that is a correct statement of a correct principle or not. In this case these two parties have entered into a contract which is subversive of the interests of a third party, namely, the public. I say that no such contract is good in law ; and when we demand that it shall not be recognized, we are not infringing in any degree on the legal or moral rights of any one. There is no necessity for a reference to any court for a decision on such a point. There are cases of right and wrong which are so plain that the duty of parliament is clear, no matter whether by one quibble of law or another it be possible to carry the case to the courts. This parliament Is here to make the law, to establish courts and, above all, to see that justice is done.

My hon. friend the Minister of Justice says the law is on the statute and the proper thing to do, is not to question it, but let the courts determine whether it is legal or not. But is it not very common for us to say that the law is and always has been so and so, and that that is what the law was intended to be ? When we have made a law and we find that, in the carrying out of that law, an interpretatioh is put upon it which is not according to the intention of parliament, parliament very often steps in and explains that Act, and says that the law was intended to be so and so, and is so and so. That is what we could do without doing any injustice to the people, c(r parliament, or vested rights.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) has drawn attention to something that may be called a grievance with respect to the telephone question. But the remedy for that grievance will not be fqund in the usurpation by parliament of functions which do not belong to it. There are some 'gentlemen in this House who, when they discuss a question of this sort, call it legal quibbling to speak about the sanctity of contracts. Well, my hon. friends may call it what they like, so far as I am concerned-and I believe so far as the great majority of thinking people are concerned-one of the fundamental principles of parliamentary government is that we must hold sacred by our covenants and see that other people do likewise. I think that a scheme may be devised, before this Bill is disposed of, by which we may arrange that, with respect to the future, no contract such as the one now at issue between the municipalities of Port Arthur and Fort William and the Canadian Pacific Railway and Bell Telephone companies can be made which will be binding on the outside public. But with respect to the contract already in existence, I will be no party to the violation of that contract or to the protection of any party who desires to break his engagements.
But the Minister of Finance said last night that parliament was the proper place.

Under this amendment, the Grand Trunk Railway would have to give a rate of two and a half cents per mile ; and, in a very few years, judging by the increase of its traffic, it would have to come down to a two-cent rate. Those portions of the Canadian Pacific Railway that are outside of the original agreement between the syndicate ancf the government would have to give the public the same rate by reason of the law of competition. The supreme reason I give for this amendment is this: That all these roads, the Grand Trunk, the Canadian Pacific and the Michigan Central, are to-day carrying all the traffic that originates in the United States and passes over their lines, whether east or w'est, at a rate of two cents per mile or less, and yet they charge Canadians riding in the same cars three cents per mile and over. I say this is most Iniquitous conduct on the part of these great railroads that have been so heavily subsidized by the Canadian people. X have already laid all these considerations before parliament. The House is seized of the facts. So also are the public, who, I believe will insist on this reform being carried out.
Furthermore, it has been proven-and the facts can easily be given-that wherever there has been a reduction of railway rates the earnings of the railways have been increased. No company in the United States that has passed under the regulations of these laws governing rates can show that it has suffered in the least; on the contrary the facts all go to prove what the experts, especially those connected with the Interstate Commerce Commission, declare, that the results are favourable to the railway. The same principle has been established in connection with the post office ; it has been established in connection with the telegraph system of various countries, it has been established above all, in connection with the railway systems of Europe-that if you reduce the cost, the public use the service so extensively that the earnings are actually increased. It is clear, therefore, that parliament would be doing no injustice by compelling these roads to reduce their passenger rates. As I have said, all I ask is to define the standard passenger tariff for which provision has alfeady been made in the statute. If the government think well to make a four-cent rate for the roads that earn very little money, I shall have no objection. This law will have the effect of reducing the rates upon those great roads that have plenty of traffic. If there is any company doing a good business in this country, the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific are doing a good business in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. Their trains are crowded, and they are constantly Mr. MACLEAN.
increasing the number of their trains. They did an immense business when they reduced the rates some time ago by reason of competition, and the same result will follow if the rates are reduced by statute. We have already carried out this system in connection with the Intercolonial. To-day the people's railway gives the people a two-cent rate. And, in the province of Manitoba the people have a three-eent rate. Yet, in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec the Grand Trunk is actually charging from three and a quarter cents to three and a half cents per mile for a considerable proportion ot the travel. The Canadian Pacific Railway is charging four cents per mile between here and the St. Lawrence on one of its branches. Surely the time has come when the standard passenger rate should be fixed. I have produced a great deal of evidence before the House and before the Committee on Railways and Canals in support of this amendment. I have not, so far, met with anything that seems to me to justify a change in the opinion I hold on the subject. It seems clear to me that no injustice would be done to the railways if we compelled them to reduce their passenger rates. I therefore submit this amendment in the hope that parliament will adopt it and that the Minister of Railways will assist me in defining the maximum passenger rate of this country.

I think the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) is entitled to a great deal of credit for having brought this question before parliament so persistently, both in this and previous sessions. I think it must be generally agreed that if passengers can be carried profitably at a two-cent rate under similar conditions in the states, it is a fair proposition that they might be carried at the same rate in Canada. There is no doubt that in Canada we are entitled to all the benefits that come from the operation of railroads which exist very largely by reason of public moneys paid them by the people of the country. At the same time I think it would be fair to consider that last year parliament established a Railway Commission empowered to deal with the question of railway passenger rates, and given almost unlimited powers in this matter. I think it would be well to wait and see w'hat the Railway Commission will clo in this matter before parliament takes action directly. While I have no doubt that the hon. member for East York lias gone very carefully into this subject of railway rates and is probably satisfied in his own mind of the correctness of his contention, a large majority of us have not done so. At any rate, it must be admitted that the members of the Railway Commission are in a position, and it is part of their duty, to inform themselves on this subject, while many in this House have not been able so to inform themselves ; and I am
