prepared to say that if the Railway Commission does not in good time take action on this question it will he necessary then for the House to take action. Certainly circumstances look in that direction. At the same time, the danger of taking drastic action without due consideration is evidenced in some degree by the results on the Intercolonial. We have a two-cent rate on the Intercolonial, and we have a deficit of half a million dollars on the Intercolonial. Therefore I think the rate on the Intercolonial is rather an argument against the proposition of the hon. gentleman than in favour of it.
Another point worthy of consideration is that there are different classes of rates, there is the first-class rate and the second-class rate. I do not know how the reduction of the first-class rate to two cents might affect the second-class rate. At the present time people who can afford it pay the high rate, those who cannot afford to pay the high rate pay a lower rate. I do not think it would be right that those who could afford the higher rate should be permitted to travel at the lower rate, and those who get the benefit of the still lower rate at the present time be compelled to pay a higher rate than they do now. That is, however, a question that could be dealt with by the commission, and it is one that I do not consider myself in a position at the present time to deal with to the extent of endorsing the hon. gentleman's proposition. Another thing that inspires me with doubt in regard to this matter was the remark made by the hon. member that if proportionate reductions were made on roads of heavy travel he would not object to a corresponding increase of the rates on roads where the travel was proportionately light. Representing a part of the country where settlement is sparse and where the travel on newly constructed roads is likely to be light for a few years, I am afraid I could hardly follow him in that jiroposition.
Don't you pay four cents there now ?

We used to pay five cents, but it is reduced to four, and in Manitoba it is three cents. At the same time, if the rate is fixed according to traffic, it is perfectly clear that a new road through a lightly settled country would possibly have to charge a much higher price.
Not if it is owned by the same corporation.

I am afraid that the basis is perhaps hardly fair when you work it out to a conclusion and apply it under all conditions all over the country. Therefore, I cannot for the present take the responsibility of voting for the amendment of the hon. member, although I think he is entitled to a great deal of credit in his effort ; and if a remedy is not found by the Railway Commission in due time it will be necessary for parliament to take even the direct action he has suggested, even perhaps without as full information as is desirable. But we must all agree, in line with the discussion we have had, that a public grievance requires a public remedy.
Mr SPROTJiLE When the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) introduced this subject some time ago and proposed to make a general two-cent rate all over the country, I refused to support him on the ground that in my judgment the railways in sparsely settled parts of the country where the earnings are small, could scarcely be expected to give a two-cent rate. At that time the suggestion was made that provided the railroads east of Port Arthur gave a two-cent rate, west of that, which was a new country, where the traffic was comparatively light, they might charge whatever rates the law allowed them to charge. But I was always of the opinion that it would be an injustice to the railways to make them carry passengers for two cents a mile when the earnings were small and the passenger traffic was light. The experience of railways in the United States, and the experience 'of the American people in compelling railways, especially in Michigan and the west, a country similar to Canada, to carry passengers at two cents a mile when their earnings were $3,000 a mile or over, has been fairly successful, and it has wrought no great injustice to the railways and has been a concession to the people. When this subject was discussed in the Railway Committee some time ago, we had representatives of the railway companies before us, and I did not understand from any of them that they seriously complained because the roads were compelled to carry passengers at two cents a mile where they were earning $3,000 a mile. But their contention was that the member for East York had misrepresented the facts that really existed in the eastern states, or in the state* of Michigan, because he had said that all the railways there carried passengers for two cents a mile. They contended that that was not the case, and they gave us a list of those railways that did carry passengers at two cents a mile and those that did not. The railways that did carry passengers at that rate were compelled to do so by virtue of the Michigan law, but they did not contend that the law was doing a great injustice to the railways. Now, if the experience in Michigan, a country similar to eastern Canada, is that passengers can be carried at two cents a mile when the earnings reach $3,000 a mile, it can be no great injustice or hardship to ask railway companies to do the same here, because, we have given a great deal more money to assist in building railways than the Michigan people have done. We tax them lighter in ordinary municipal taxation, and we give

them many concessions that the American people do not. Now, the hon. member for East York proposes a graded tariff, and I think no great injustice would be done to the railways provided parliament adopted that proposition.
The hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) says that the Intercolonial Railway gives a two cent rate per mile, and as a consequence it has a deficit of nearly half a million dollars last year. If I could reach the conclusion that the deficit was due to carrying passengers at two cents a mile it would be to me an argument, but there are many elements in the situation that effect it, and which help to make a deficit of half a million other than the carrying of passengers at two cents a mile. In my judgment it is other elements in the situation that have brought about this deficit in the earnings of the road and not the carrying passengers at [DOT]two cents a mile. I do not think that seriously affects it in any sense. But then we are asked to wait for the action of the Railway Commission. The Railway Commission have extensive powers. I assume that the Railway Commission are not likely to ask the railway companies to carry passengers jat a very much lower rate than that which they are charging to-day. It may be said that it is generally conceded that three cents a mile is a fair charge and that they are {not likely to ask them to carry passengers for very much less than that. I do not think we would be doing very much injustice to the Railway Commission, or that we would be curtailing their powers in any way or interfering with their functions if we laid down the salutary principle which has been found fairly satisfactory in Michigan and asked the railway companies, when their earnings reached a maximum of $3,000 a mile as the case may be, to carry passengers at a graded rate in proportion to their earnings. If we did that I think we would be doing them no injustice and therefore I am inclined to support the amendment of my hon. friend from East York.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As this matter has been very fully discussed both in this House and in the Railway Committee I do not think the time of the committee can be very usefully taken up with a lengthy discussion of the subject. But I would like to direct attention to section 26-1 of the Railway Act which says that the Railway Commissioners shall adopt a standard passenger tariff for the whole of Canada. No passenger rates can be collected by any railway company in Canada which comes under the operation of this Act except under the standard passenger tariff which has been fixed by (he Railway Commission. Let us give the Railway Commission that was established under the statute passed last session, time to do something under the provisions of that Act before we proceed liere to determine what Mr. SPROULE.
they are to do. It seems to me that having created this Railway Commission for the purpose of regulating this question we should give them an opoprtunity to do it. I think it is not only important to draw attention to that feature of the law as we have it today, but it is also important to disabuse the public mind of the impression that exists that a two cent rate is now in force in the state of Michigan and in tbe state of New York. That is not correct. I will state the law as it is in Michigan and as it is in New York and I will show that the law in the state of Michigan does not apply to more than one-third of the railways in Michigan.
And to how much of the traffic ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Allow me. On the Michigan Central a two cent rate applies only to the main line between Detroit and the Indiana state line, a distance of 221 miles, on the Toledo division between Toledo and the Ohio state line, a distance of 46 miles and on the Grand Rapids division between Jackson and Grand Rapids a distance of 95 miles, or altogether a total of 362 miles out of 1,137 miles in the state. My hon. friend knows perfectly well that under the terms of filie statute which I read to him when this matter was before the Railway Committee the law is only applicable to those railways which are within the limits of the southern portion of the state of Michigan. It does not apply to the railways in the northern part of the state of Michigan. The railways there operate to a large extent under tlie same conditions as those which exist in Canada.
Why does it not apply to Alpena or the Peninsula ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot say why, because it is for the legislature that passed the law to say and not for me. They have found it proper not to apply the law Jo the northern part of the state.
The representative of the railway company said before fihe committee that it was because their earnings did not come up to $3,000 a mile.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know what was said before the Railway Committee. I am stating what the law is in the state of Michigan. That law applies simply to the railways in the southern part of the state, which I have mentioned. In respect to the state of New York there is no general statute fixing the two cent rate but a two cent maximum rate was fixed on that portion of the road between Albany and Buffalo and that rate was fixed forty years ago for the purpose of impeding the construction of the New York Central which at that time was competing for business with the Erie canal, the Erie Canal being owned by the state. As a mattter of fact the general rate in force in the New York state is 3 cents a mile.
Does the hon. gentleman state that ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
I say he is misinformed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I endeavour as far as posible not to make reckless statements here. I say now to my hon. friend that the two cent rate was fixed by the statute forty years ago, that statute can be found in the consolidation statutes of the state of New York, and I repeat that that rate is only applicable to the line between Albany and Buffalo.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is only applicable to the line between Albany and Buffalo. There is no general rate of two cents a mile in the state of New York.
Not under the law but in the practice of the companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am talking of something we are sure of, something we can control. We cannot control statements as to what the practice is in reference to these roads. I do not wish to say that my hon. friend would lead us astray, but we have to take the statements of those who are interested in the management of the traffic on these roads and as these statements are not at all times accurate my Iron, friend may be under a wrong impression. In respect to the state of New York, there is no law fixing a two cent rate except that which I have mentioned and it is only applicable to the portion of the line .between Albany and Buffalo. I heard it suggested this afternoon by some one that we were obstructing our own legislation on this side of the House and to avoid following the bad example that has been given I will not say anything further.

I am only going to say two or three words in answer to the hon. Minister of Justice. I repeated to-day and I repeat again now that under the legislation that exists in the state of Michigan ninety per cent of the passenger traffic is carried for two cents and less than two cents, a mile and that the result of the legislation in New York state is that more than ninety per cent of the traffic in New York state not only on the New York Central but on the Erie, the Lehigh Valley and a portion of the Pennsylvania system is carried at two cents a mile. My contention is that the Grand Trunk Railway Company, when they give to the people of Michigan a rate of two cents a mile, ought to do the same thing in Canada because we have here a country of a similar character. The New York Central Railway Company are carrying people in Michigan for two cents a mile and I contend that they ought to carry them in Ontario for two cents
a mile. In the province of Manitoba they have a three cent rate over the whole of that province. Why ? Because the Canadian Northern have to give that rate by reason of a little agreement that they have with the government of Manitoba. Then, we are asked to wait until we see what this commission do. What are the facts ? Until I put a question on the order paper the other day asking what railways had complied with this law which ordered them to file their standard passenger tariffs, not one road had done it, and to-day not one road has done it and they have had to go to the commission, by reason of the agitation that I have carried on, and to ask an extension of time until November to enable them to file their passenger tariffs. That is what we will get if we leave it to the Railway Commission. There will be no standard passenger tariffs filed, the commission will say that they are too busily engaged with other things and nothing at all will be done. I accept what the hon. Minister of Justice has said and I close the discussion as far as I am concerned, but on Tuesday next I propose to divide the House on this very issue of a regulated and reduced passenger rate.

It has been asserted, as an argument in favour of a two-cent rate, that with a rate of two cents a mile for passenger traffic the railways would earn a great deal more money than with a three-cent rate. It is a sux*prise to me that men like Sir Rivers-Wilson, C. M. Hays, Sir Thomas Shaughnessy and other great railway men never discovered that fact. I think if they really believed that this was the case, they would no doubt at once offer the people of this country a lower rate for passenger traffic. My position is this. I have voted for a two-cent rate in this House perhaps almost before the hon. member for East York came into parliament, at any rate, before he became as prominent in railway legislation as he is now, so that this is not a new question to me. My desire is to see the people of this country gel the cheapest possible railway travel, and I desire to proceed along that line which wifi secure a reduction in railway rates at the earliest possible date. Whichever plan is likely to succeed the better and to bring about a modification in the direction of cheaper rates at the earlier date I am prepared to adopt. If the hon, member for East York can show me that the plan proposed by his amendment is likely to give us better rates in the near future than we can possibly get through the Railway Commission, to whom this matter is to be submitted, then I would fall in line with the suggestion made by him ; but if I realized that through the Railway Commission a reduction in rates could be secured at an earlier date than under the system proposed by this amendment, then I would be willing to wait

and see what the Railway Commission would do.
I find that the Canadian Pacific Railway, in 1896, earned only $766 per mile by passenger traffic on their entire system. In 1903 their earnings from this source amounted to $1,460, an increase in round numbers of $700 in seven years, or at the rare of $100 per year. At the same rate of increase it would still require fifteen years for the Canadian Pacific Railway to reach the $3,000 per mile mark. That is a long time to wait for a good many of us. If the Canadian Pacific Railway earnings do not increase more rapidly during the next period of seven years, or the two next succeeding periods of seven years, than they have been increasing in the past, then we cannot at all expect that we will arrive at the goal of $3,000 per mile inside of fifteen years. Have we any reason to anticipate that the Canadian Pacific Railway earnings for passenger travel will increase more rapidly in the next fifteen years, or in the next seven years, than they have done in the past seven years'? We have had seven years of what the Finance Minister calls unprecedented prosperity in this country. We have had a prosperous seven years. Is it likely that the same condition will continue during the next seven years ? Periods of prosperity and adversity usually come in cycles. Some years ago the Finance Minister told us that we were on the crest of the wave and that we must prepare for adversity. All the arguments we have heard in speeches from various sources would lead us to assume that we must not expect a continuance of the same prosperity in this country during the next fifteen years as we have had during the past seven years. We have often been reminded that in the United States, whilst a wave of prosperity has been felt over the whole world, a period of adversity has even now set in there, so that the United States railways would not reasonably expect, under conditions of that kind, to earn as much money, because they share in the prosperity or adversity of the country ; they make more money during prosperous times than during times that are not prosperous. The same thing would apply to Canadian railways. During prosperous times people would travel more and the earnings of our railways would be greater than in times of hardship. Therefore, I say we have no reason whatever to hope that the earnings of the Canadian Pacific Railway will be greater per annum during the next seven years than they have been in the past seven years, and at the rate of increase that they have had during the last seven years, it would take fifteen years to reach the goal of $3,000 per mile.
So much then for the Canadian Pacific Railway ; let us take the other great railway system in Canada, the Grand Trunk Railway. In 1896 their earnings were $1,600 per mile. In 1903, after a period of seven Mr. HENDERSON.
years of prosperity in Canada, when, no doubt, the Grand Trunk Railway earned every additional dollar that the prosperous times would bring to them, their earnings were $2,200 per mile, an increase of $600, not as large an increase as that of the Canadian Pacific Railway, an increase of only about $85 per year. Now, the railway would have to continue to increase its passenger earnings until it reached the goal of $3,000 per mile before the general public would have the convenience of a two-cent rate, and at the same rate of increase it would take about nine years to reach the $3,000 per mile so as to give the public the two-cent rate. Even nine years is a considerable time to wait, but we have to consider the fact that we have had seven years of prosperous times, with the possibility that the next seven years, or the next nine years will not be so productive of results as the past seven years have been. Therefore, instead of being nine years it might possibly be ten or twelve years. We have no guarantee that it will be brought about in nine years. Now, let us look at the two positions. Shall we legislate along the lines indicated by the hon. member for East York, or along some other line that would compel the railways to give transportation at a reduced rate, and fix that rate if we thought fit to do so? Having committed the whole of this matter within the past twelve months to a Railway Commission, who would have power to deal with the matter, to look into all the circumstances and decide as to whether the railways were entitled to give cheaper transportation or not, should we leave it to that commission ? Two plans are before us, and it is for us now to decide which of these two plans is the more likely to bring about the result we desire at the earlier day. I have no hesitation in saying to-night that I think we have reason to expect that through the Railway Commission we will get relief at an earlier date than we would by adopting a measure that would postpone the reduction to a period so very remote. That is my impression, and I would be very sorry to place on the statute-books of this country a law which would establish a rate that could not come into operation for ten or fifteen years, when I have hopes that through the Railway Commission better results would be obtained in a much shorter period of time. Nothing is to be lost by allowing the Railway Commission to deal with the matter during the next year or two, and see how they can work out this whole matter. The proposition of the hon. member for East York-and he has put his case forcibly and intelligently before the public-cannot come into operation for from ten to fifteen years.
It would come into operation to-morrow in connection with the Michigan Central and the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Not with regard to the two-cent rate.
The two and a halt cent rate is my proposition.

There is no great hardship at present on that account, because any man can travel on the Grand Trunk or the Canadian Pacific Railway for two and a half cents a mile by purchasing a return ticket. It may' be said that that compels a man to return by the same route. Well,
I have no doubt that ninety per cent of the people who go from home on a journey come back again. So that there is not so much to be gained by the hon. gentleman's proposition for a two and a half cent rate as perhaps the general public might think without looking fairly into the matter. If a man has a great deal of travel to do as a commercial traveller, he can do so at two and a quarter cents a mile ; or any men or woman w*ho has considerable travelling to do in this country can travel at two and a half cents a mile on the Canadian Pacific Railway and I think on the Grand Trunk Railway by purchasing a thousand-mile ticket for twenty-five dollars. It would not take very much travelling to use that up, perhaps only from Toronto to Quebec and return. But suppose a man were travelling around the country on some business that necessitated his going one way and returning another, he could travel at two and a half cents a mile by purchasing a thousand-mile ticket for twenty-five dollars, and he is allowed twelve months in which to use it up. In all probability he would use it up in that time, and perhaps a good deal more. Even in the state of Michigan, I understand that for a short distance, even where the rate is fixed at two cents a mile, the actual rate is three cents. However, that is not a matter of very great importance. I trust I have made myself plain to the House. I am prepared to adopt whatever plan is most likely to bring about the desired result at the earliest period. If I did not believe that through the Railway Commission we could realize the goal of two cents a mile or a reduced rate at an earlier date than we could by placing this amendment on the statute-book. I would fall into line readily with some such plan as that suggested by the hon. member for East York. But I realize that we can lose nothing by waiting for a year or two for the result of the Railway Commission's investigation, before we take action of this kind; because, even if we passed a Bill this week fixing a rate of two cents a mile on railways earning .$3,000 a mile, it would not come into operation on the great railways of this country for a considerable number of years. I have an impression that under the Railway
Act the Railway Commision have power to give a reduced rate in certain parts of the country where railway passenger traffic is very much greater, while not reducing it in other sections of the country where the pasenger traffic is more moderate.
Under what clause is that ?

Under clause 263. I would like to have the opinion of the Minister of Justice on that clause read in connection with clause 264. It does seem to me that the words are broad enough to give the Railway Commission power to take all the circumstances into consideration, and in a thickly settled portion of the province to give a reduced rate, while allowing the rate to remain as it is, or fixing a higher rate, in other and more sparsely settled portions of the province. Knowing that through the county I have the honour to represent there is about as much passenger travel as through any other county in Ontario,. I would be sony to fix the lower rate at a figure- that would not come into operation for ten or fifteen years. I have hopes that the Railway Commission inside of a year or two will give us relief that we could not obtain in the other wav except by waiting a very long time. These are the views I hold. The hon. member says be will divide the House on the question. I hope to be here when the House is divided upon it. It is a question which I have no fear to meet, and I am going to vote upon it in accordance with the views whiCh I have expressed and for what seems to me to afford a most reasonable hope or securing a lower rate, and securing it at the earliest possible time.

My views on this question are so well known that it will not be necessary for me to repeat them. But I desire to draw the attention of the House to the unsound business principle that underlies the resolution. This reduction of the railway rate to two cents a mile is supposed to apply to railways earning $3,000 a mile. The only railway in the country that is earning $3,000 a mile is the railway that is the least able to reduce its passenger rate. On an invested capital of $35,000,000 in the Canadian Southern Railway, the actual net earnings last year amounted to $111,000 or less than one-third of one per cent.
The presumption that where a railway is earning $3,000 per mile, it is in a position to reduce its rates, is entirely fallacious. It does not follow that because a railway company is earning $3,000 or $2,500 a mile, it is more able to reduce its rates than a company which is earning less than one-half that amount. The largest earner in the country per mile is the Canada Southern, vet the actual amount of its net earnings was $111,000 or less than one-third of one

per cent. Take the Grand Trunk Railway, the only one to which the two and a half per cent would apply, and we find that on an invested capital of $335,000,000, the actual net earnings are $8,000,000 or less than three per cent. Although apparently a wealthy railway company, it is not able to reduce its passenger rates, because its net earnings give less than three per cent on the capital invested. It does not follow that because railways are large money earners, they are better able to reduce their passenger rates to two cents per mile than other railways which earn less. Therefore the very foundation of the hon. member's resolution disappears because the railways to which it would apply are those least able to stand a reduction.
Amendment (Mr. Maclean) negatived.
On section 1,
Notwithstanding anything contained in the Railway Act, 1903, the Governor in Council shall have, and shall be deemed to have had since the date upon which the said Act came into force, power, authority and jurisdiction to sanction, confirm, rescind, change or vary, or to take other action upon, any report, order or decision of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council made before the said date under the Railway Act of 1888, or any Act in amendment thereof, in as full and ample a manner as if the Railway Act, 1903, had not been passed, or had not come into force, and as if the said Railway Act of 1888 and the said Acts in amendment thereof had not been repealed ; and any order or decision so sanctioned or confirmed shall have the same validity, force and effect as if the said order or decision had been so sanctioned or confirmed prior to the issue thereof.
Are we not proposing to do what very eminent authorities on that side have said we should not do. and that is attempt to say what the law was intended to be and what it is ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Nothing of the sort.

I want to draw the attention^ to the fifth line. I understand that the object of the section is to enable certain orders of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council to be confirmed. Owing to the change made by the Act last year, there are some orders of the old Privy Council Committee which have not been confirmed and which the Governor General in Council cannot now confirm without a new Act. But I do not see why the minister should take power to the Governor General in Council not only to sanction and confirm these orders, but should continue in him the right for all time hereafter to rescind, change, vary or take other action upon them. I would submit that the proper way would be to take power to sanction and confirm them, when confirmed that they should be under the same provisions as if they had been enacted by the Board of Railway Commissioners.

I would suggest therefore that you strike out the words ' rescind, change or vary or take other action upon ' from the fifth line, and after the word ' effect ' in the third line from the bottom of the clause insert the words ' and be subject to the provisions of the Railway Act of 1903' and strike out the words ' issue thereof ' at the end of the clause and insert instead ' passing of the last mentioned Act.'
I have given the minister the section altered as I propose. I think that would answer his purpose. It would enable the Governor General in Council to make valid all the orders and regulations that have not yet been confirmed, and after they are confirmed they would then come under the ordinary jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) has very correctly stated the object of this legislation. But I would like to draw his attention to this point. The attention of the government is to restore the powers of the Governor General in Council with respect to orders made by the Railway Committee so that these powers may be the same as they were previous to the repeal of the old Act. At present there is but one order of the Railway Committee to deal with, the order with respect to the Yonge street crossing at Toronto. That is the order we have in our mind, and I think it is important we should restore to the Governor General in Council all the powers he had previous to the new Act which repealed the old Railway Act of 1888. These powers are all conferred not only by section .187 of the Railway Act, but also by section 21-1 am speaking now of the old Railway Act. If my hon. friend will look at section 21 and read that in connection with section 187, he will see that the Governor in Council had the authority to sanction, confirm, rescind or vary. It might be important that the order should be changed to a slight extent to meet altered circumstances, and in that view we desire to have the old jurisdiction restored. With respect to the other words 'to take other action upon ' it might be found desirable to refer the matter again for further consideration to the Railway Commission. That is the reason these words are in the section. With respect to my hon. friend's amendment, its last part is, I think, an improvement on the terms we use.
Have the parties to the particular order to which the hon. gentleman refers approved of this ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. The only party that has been consulted is the city of Toronto. The amendment was submitted to them and they approved of it. They approved of the concluding words, but I take the responsibility of making the change because I think it is an improvement without altering the sense.

The Minister of Justice contradicted the statement I made that the object of this was to declare what the Act was intended to mean. It seems to me the words mean nothing if my interpretation is not correct. What else can these words mean-' notwithstanding anything contained in the Railway Act, 1903, the Governor in Council shall have and shall be deemed to have had since that date '-and so on, if they do not mean to interpret the law and declare what it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Section 187 of the Railway Act of 1888 provided that the Railway Committee, if it appeared to them expedient or necessary for the public safety was empowered, from time to time, with the sanction of the Governor in Council, to authorize or require a company owning a railway constructed upon, along or across any street or other public highway at rail level or otherwise, to carry such street or highway over or under the said railway by means of a bridge or arch, instead of crossing at rail level, or to divert such street highway either temporarily or pei'manently, or to execute such other work and take such other measures, as, under the circumstances of the case, appeared to the Railway Committee best adapted to remove or diminish the danger arising from the then position of the railway. It will be observed that an order made under that section required the approval of the Governor in Council to have validity and effect. The Railway Act of 1903. abolishes the'Railway Committee. And section 310 of the Railway Act of 1903 repeals the Railway Act of 1888. So that, while the committee has passed the order, the order had no validity and effect because the Governor in Council was without power to deal with the matter. This is, therefore, not to interpret, to construe, but it is to restore the power of the Governor in Council with regal'd to these orders to what it would have been if there had been no repeal.
It is intended to apply to something that has not been completed. What is it ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The Yonge street crossing in Toronto, in which the city of Toronto, the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific Railway are all interested. The Railway Committee of the Privy Council made an order authorizing the construction of an overhead bridge or some other form of crossing and determined the share which each of the parties interested should contribute toward the construction and maintenance. And, of course, that order of the Railway Committee has no validity because the Governor in Council has no power to deal with it.
Section, as amended, agreed to.
On section 2,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Briefly, this section is intended to apply to railways that are
situated entirely within the limits of one province and that would be under the exclusive jurisdiction of that province were it not for the fact that they have been declared to be works for the general advantage of Canada and to provide that they shall be subject to the Sunday legislation of the province in which they are.
As I understand it, this is to place them under the control of the legislature in reference to Sunday observance alone.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Exclusively. And, in order to make that absolutely clear, i propose the following amendment:
This section shall not apply to any railway or part of a railway which forms part of a continuous route or system operated between two or more provinces or between any province and a foreign country or to any railway or part of a railway between any of the ports on the great lakes and such continuous route or system, nor shall it apply to any part of a railway which the Governor in Council, may by proclamation declare to be exempt from the provisions of this section.
The intention is to exempt from the operation of the law the Canadian Southern which forms part of the through system of the Michigan Central with respect to its traffic and also part of the Canadian Pacific which,
I understand, operates between a port on the great lakes-Owen Sound, I believe- and the city of Toronto, and other railways that are part of through continuous systems and which are not, properly speaking, local enterprises at all and which we think, should not have this law applied to them.

I would ask the minister how far this section will apply to many of these short lines now forming part of the Grand Trunk corporation, but which were originally local railways and declared works for the general advantage of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is a difficulty that I mean to meet by this amendment.
There are several such lines in Ontario.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

I would like to call the attention of the minister to subsection 2. It seems to be very unusual and extraordinary legislation. It reads :
The Governor in Council may at any time and from time to time by proclamation confirm, for the purposes of this section any Act of the legislature of any province passed after -the passing of this Act for the prohibition or regulation of work, business or labour upon the first day of the week.
That looks like giving a power of attorney to the ministers to get the local legislatures to pass Acts which the ministers will make into law. A local legislature may hereafter pass laws upon this subject and

we authorize the Governor in Council to make them valid.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will point out our difficulties. Under the first paragraph we approve of the Sunday legislation now in existence. We know the legislation, anti knowing it we declare it unobjectionable and we approve of it. Now, with respect to future legislation that may be passed- because after all these laws affecting Sunday may be changed by the local legislatures at any time-with respect to them, it seems to me it would not be wise for this parliament to say that we approve in advance of any legislation which may be passed by any province. The only other alternative is fo give to the Governor in Council authority by proclamation to declare that any Act respecting the observance of Sunday passed by a local legislature should be confirmed and ratified, so far as that Act may be within the limits and powers conferred upon the province. We have either one or the other thing to do, either to confirm in advance legislation of the character of which we must necessarily be in ignorance, or else to give to the Governor in Council authority and power to ratify and confirm that legislation when it has passed.
Can we delegate that power to the Governor in Council ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No. We could not delegate it, but we give the Governor in Council power to adopt. It is not a delegation, it is an adoption of the legislation of the province and making it our own.

Surely it is delegating power to the Governor in Council to confirm an Act which we do not know the effect of.
On section 3,

I have given to the Minister of Justice a copy of an amendment that I propose to suggest on this section. I propose to add some words after the words ' An Act to amend the National Transcontinental Railway Act ' in the fifth line. The section as it is now printed is limited to the purpose of ascertaining the true net earnings of the eastern division of the leased portion of the Transcontinental Railway. But in drawing the section it seems to me the fact was overlooked that so long as the government is guarantor of the bonds upon the western division, it is equally interested in seeing that the Grand Trunk Pacific should receive a proper portion of the through earnings as regards the whole of its system. It is just as much interested in seeing that the Grand Trunk Company gives the Grand Trunk Pacific a fair proportion of the through rate for the whole of the railway as it is interested in seeing that we shall get a fair portion as regards the leased or eastern division. Scr I propose to add these words :
And in order to the ascertainment of the true net earnings of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company upon its system of railways at ail times while the principal or interest of 'any bonds made by the said company and guaranteed by the government of Canada shall be unpaid by the said company.
Then I propose further on to add at the end of line 19, the words :
Or as guarantor of any such principal or
interest.
Then at the end of that first section I propose to add further words. The clause provides for a fair apportionment of the rates, but before the question of determining can arise, the rates will have been divided, and the Grand Trunk Company, or the other carriers who are interested in through rates, will have received their share, and the clause does not provide for the payment or repayment to the Grand Trunk Pacific of what it has been short of in the division. I propose that the Grand Trunk Railway Company shall make that good, whatever ihe shortage is, because the Grand Trunk Railway Company is given absolute control over the Grand Trunk Pacific, and if it allows them to receive too little of the through rate, the Grand Trunk itself should make good what the Grand Trunk Pacific may lose. I therefore propose to add that:
The Grand Trunk Railway Company shall pay "to fhe Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company such sum and sums of money as, by the said board, from time to time may be ascertained to be necessary to make good the true net earnings upon the basis aforesaid of the said eastern division, and of the said Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company's system of railways.
Provided always that either party to any such question may appeal from any such determination to the Supreme Court of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: When the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Act was up for consideration it was pointed out that under the Railway Act as we have it now there was no power vested in the Railway Commission to determine the question of a joint tariff between the two companies, that the two companies were free to make such a joint tariff as might suit their own convenience and that as a result of the powers so vested in these two companies the Grand Trunk Railway Company might he in a position to practically divert all the traffic down by North Bay, make a through-rate and send the whole of the traffic to Portland as at the present time. In order to prevent that I promised to introduce legislation which would enable the Railway Commission to deal with this question of a joint tariff. That has been done and accomplished by the amendment as I now introduce it. My hon. friend (Mr. Barker) is anxious to go somewhat farther and to give the Railway Commission power to make an investigation in respect to the ascertain-

meiit of tlie true uet earnings of the western division so that the government may know in respect to its obligation as guarantor what the true obligations are. 1 argued at the time the question was up before that these powers were already vested in the Railway Commission under sections 45 and 309 of the Railway Act and that it was not necessary to have that amendment, but,
I think, to be strictly logical, having advanced the contention that these powers were already vested in the Railway Commissioners and as there will be no objection to our reaffirmation of it in this legislation in respect to the amendment of my hon. friend to that section I accept it, but in respect to the last part of the amendment imposing an* obligation on the company to pay over so much I think that would be a departure from the original contract and I cannot accept it.

The reason I ask it is this : The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company will not be in existence in the operation of the road. It will be a mere name. The Grand Trunk Railway Company itself will make the rates, collect the rates and divide the rates. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company will never be heard of in the practical operation of the road. The Grand Trunk Railway Company can give itself for its own line more than is fair or reasonable and it may have an object in view in making, as to the eastern division, the line not pay its interest in which case it would not have to pay the rent. It might have an object in making the whole line, including the western division, not paying because it might be interested at some time in putting the bonds that this government has guaranteed in default. It may be no injustice to the Grand Trunk Railway proper which has the whole control and which makes the unfair apportionment of the rate to compel it to make It good so that the company which the government has guaranteed may receive its due share of the through-rate. I will add that it means more than what the hon. Minister of Justice has said as to a diversion of the traffic to North Bay. It is equally important that there should be a fair apportionment if the traffic that goes to Quebec and thence to some point on the Grand Trunk Railway,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, that is quite right. I had not thought of that.

There is no question about that. I may say again that the general Railway Act cannot apply practically because these sections in the general Railway Act are intended to apply where there are two companies with an opposing interest and one complains that it was not getting a fair share, but nobody ever supposes that 216
there will be any complaint between the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Railway Company when they get into operation. It is only one company and the section of the general Railway Act will never be brought into play at all. There will be no complaint. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company will never appear before the Board of Railway Commissioners to complain that its parent, the Grand Trunk Railway Company, is not doing it justice. You will never hear from the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway at all. Therefore, these sections in the general Railway Act cannot apply and it is for that reason that the greatest care has to be taken in the interest of the government that it should have the power to see that the rates may be fairly apportioned and that the Grand Trunk Railway Company shall make good to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company the loss occasioned by an unfair apportionment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have faithfully lived up to the pledge I gave at the time the National Transcontinental Railway Act was under consideration by the introduction of the Bill in its original form. The suggested amendment of my hon. friend in respect to an investigation into the accounts of the western division I accept because it is practically putting to the test my good faith, when I submit that it is already covered by the Railway Act, but I do not think my hon. friend could ask me to go farther.

Mr. Barker moves to add the following words in the eighth line after the word 'Act':
And in order to the ascertainment of the true net earnings of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company upon its system of railways at all times while the principal or interest of any bonds made by the said company and guaranteed by the government of Canada shall be unpaid by the said company.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

Then, again at the 19th line after the word ' railway,' Mr. Barker proposes to add the following words :
Or as guarantor of any such principal or interest.
Amendment (Mr. Barker) agreed to.

Mr. Barker moves to add at the end of the clause the following :
The Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada shall pay to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company such sum anl sums of money as, by the said board from time to time may be ascertained to be necessary to make good the true net earnings upon the basis aforesaid of the said eastern division, and of the Grand Trunk Pa-



cific Railway Company's system of railways.
Provided always that either party to any such question may appeal from any such determination to the Supreme Court of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Lost.

Before the amendment Is considered I would ask the hon. Minister of Justice whether the initiation of any proceedings for the purpose of ascertaining the due apportionment between the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Companies may be made without the consent of either of the parties?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, by the amendment.
It can be done at the request of the Minister of Railways and Canals.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This last amendment is lost.
Amendment (Mr. Barker) negatived.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I beg to move to amend that clause 3 by adding the following words :
Provided always that either party to any such question may appeal from any such determination to the Supreme Court of Canada.
On section 4,

When this section was before the committee on a former occasion, it was suggested, I do not know whether by myself or by some other hon. gentleman on this side of the House, that this clause should read :
The majority of the directors and of the executive committee of any company, &c.
I would suggest that that should be added.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I must confess that in so far as I am personally concerned, I have absolutely no sympathy with legislation of this description. I think that if foreigners choose to come into this country and invest their money in our railways they are entitled to have some control over the railway system which is created by their capital. It seemed to me that the sense of the House then was in favour of a change in the law along these lines, and I have as a consequence introduced an amendment which will require that all railway companies, aided by the parliament of Canada, shall have a majority of their directors British subjects. With respect to the executive committee, it would appear to me that we would be pushing the matter very far if we insisted upon the executive committee coming under the same rule. These executive committees are usually composed of five members ; I think I know of one case in which the committee is composed of only three members, with the president as an ex-officio member. If we should re-Mr. CAMPBELL.
quire that a majority of this small committee shall be British subjects, it seems to me that the result would be that we would have dummies placed upon this board by the people who control the stock of the company, because, after all, the men who control the stock control the board, and the men who control the board control the executive committee. If the House would allow me to have the Bill go through in its present form, I would put my view before my colleagues, and when the Bill comes up for third reading, if it is found desirable to make an amendment we can do so.
Is anything known as an executive committee recognized by the law ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In several special Acts provision is made for an executive committee. That is the case in the special Acts of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Canadian Northern and two or three Acts passed last session. In fact, in the Grand Trunk Pacific Bill there is provision for such a committee. However, I do not want to commit the government on the subject, and I would like to have an opportunity to discuss the matter with my colleagues.
Bill, as amended, reported ; amendments read first and second time.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would be glad if the House would again facilitate the passage of the urgency Supply Bill, as to which some explanations were given both yesterday and to-day. We have been waiting until the various items were collected and put in proper form. I now move :
That the House resolve itself into Committee of Ways and Means.
Motion, agreed to, and House went into Committee of Ways and Means.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The items with which the Committee of Supply has dealt in detail in the estimates for the new fiscal year amounted to $21,585,073.78. Then, in addition to that, we have taken one-fifth of the remaining items, the amount of that one-fifth being $4,288,332.69, making the total of the sums for this coming fiscal year which have been dealt with by the committee $25,873,406.47. Accordingly I move:
Resolved, That towards making good the supply granted to His Majesty on account of certain expenses of the public service for the financial year ending the 30th of June, 1905, the sum of $25,873,406.47 be granted out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Of course, I have not verified the clerical work ; I am taking the hon. gentleman's statement and the word of his officers for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I may say that I also have to rely on the officers of the House who have done this work, and I have no reason to doubt that it is correct.
Resolution reported ; read the first and second time, and agreed to.
Mr. FIELDING moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 156) for granting to His Ma-jecty certain sums of money for the public service for the financial year ending the 30tli of June, 1905.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, Bill read the first time and the second time, considered in committee, reported, read the third time, and passed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it is rather late for us to resume the consideration of the estimates in Committee of Supply, and I move that the House do now adjourn.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the business for to-morrow ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Some of the Bills on the order paper will be taken first, and if we reach supply, the estimates of the Minister of Railways will be taken up.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 10.50 p.m.
